Through all of this, Zamir has inherited a multi-headed problem of terror emanating from the West Bank since early 2022.
He has tried to order harsher crack downs on certain more problematic Palestinian areas, reducing aspects of the terror threat substantially – by some estimates as much as 80% - but nothing close to stopping the threat.
At the same time, Zamir, along with the police, the Shin Bet, and the government more broadly, have lost control over several hundred violent Jewish extremists who have been regularly attacking both Palestinians and soldiers alike.
Zamir has not fought with Defense Minister Israel Katz to restore administrative detention of violent Jews, a tool the Shin Bet has consistently demanded be returned to them for use.
Rather, he has been strategic about public fighting with the defense minister, with a focus on keeping control of key IDF appointments and on pressing the government to draft more haredim. This has been despite pushes by Katz to make political-friendly appointments and to protect haredi political parties from any substantial concessions on drafting more young men from their sector into the military.
Possibly Zamir's most dramatic moment was a leak in March of a private speech he made to the cabinet about the need to draft more haredim in which he said, “I am raising 10 red flags before the IDF collapses into itself.”
More recently, he has also been more public lately about demanding government backing for combating Jewish extremist violence.
On August 27, Zamir announced that he was expanding the Israeli forces being used to maintain public order in the West Bank leading into the upcoming fall Jewish holidays.
The Post understands that the volume of forces will be more than double the pre-October 7 force size of around 11 battalions, which at times has grown to 15-20 battalions, but will temporarily grow even more.
Zamir warned the government that Jewish extremist violence has run out of control and that greater backing is needed from the government, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and others actively restraining political officials from provocative actions.
All of this takes place as IDF officials have said Jewish extremist violence has reached new levels, with hundreds of extremists recently drawing out a conflict with the IDF at the Palestinian village of Kusra for multiple weeks.
It also takes place as IDF and Shin Bet officials say that the police, after three years under Itamar Ben-Gvir, have reached highly problematic lows in terms of arresting and helping indict Jewish extremists in the West Bank.
None or almost none (the police have been at a low also in terms of transparency) of those involved in the Kusra actions were arrested.
Accordingly, Zamir has brought in the Golani Brigade and the Paratroopers Brigade to supplement the standard forces in the area, some of which have appeared too sympathetic to Jewish extremists attacking Palestinian villages.
However, without more backing from the government, Zamir has warned that even increased military forces will be insufficient.
Looking into 2027, in some ways, Zamir has succeeded in making Israel more secure than it was in the 2023-2025 period. But almost every front remains a challenge, such that he will continue to have his work cut out for him.

articles.title: ‘It was all hands on deck’: how the CIA responded to 9/11
articles.body:
A generation of spies had lost an enemy but not yet found a role. Then came 9/11.
A decade after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, al-Qaida’s devastating attacks on New York and Washington on 11 September 2001 announced to the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) that the long era of battling communism, for which it had been founded, was officially at an end.
It was to be replaced by a no-holds-barred “war on terror” that would leave the CIA with a soiled reputation over falsified intelligence that led to the invasion and occupation of Iraq, and an extraordinary rendition program in which suspects were subjected to “enhanced interrogations” at secret sites that official US inquiries subsequently defined as torture.
The US intelligence community was dramatically transformed after two planes flew into the World Trade Center, a third smashed into the Pentagon, and a fourth crashed in the Pennsylvania countryside after passengers overcame the hijackers.
Accounts of what unfolded inside the CIA’s headquarters in Langley, Virginia, suggests an organization unprepared for the drastically changed world the attacks ushered in, despite an awareness among some in the intelligence community that al-Qaida and its leader, Osama bin Laden, represented a clear and present danger.
Margaret Henoch, then a counter-intelligence officer with little knowledge of terrorism, recalls confusion, chaos and an initial lack of direction from senior leadership as staff struggled to process what seemed like a bolt from a clear blue sky on that balmy late summer day.
“One of my officers came in and said to me: ‘A plane just ran into the World Trade Center,’” she said. To this day, Henoch – who had previously been stationed in Vienna, where she focused on the International Atomic Energy Agency and nuclear threats – is haunted by the apparent vacuum that followed.
About 40 minutes after the first attack, with no clear direction from the top of CIA, she decided to go up to the seventh floor, which accommodated the agency’s senior figures, including its then director, George Tenet.
To her surprise, the area was deserted, apart from three assistants.
“It was reasonable that they would have moved those guys someplace else,” said Henoch. “What was unreasonable, in my humble opinion, was that no one thought about all those people sitting in that building. Because if the Pentagon was hit, there was a chance that we, too, were a target – and it would be nice to believe that the people who left the building rapidly had a thought for all those who worked for them.
“It was not clear that they did.”
The Guardian contacted Tenet, now working in the private sector, for comment. In an emailed response, Bill Harlow, the CIA’s public affairs director at the time of the attacks, cited details in the 2007 memoir, At the Center of the Storm, which he co-wrote with Tenet, and said orders were issued for the majority of the staff to leave the building at “about 10am” – nearly an hour after the second plane struck at 9.03am.
Harlow added: “We were aware at the time of intelligence gathered around 1995-96 of terrorist desires to attack CIA HQ with an airplane.
“Director Tenet and the senior leadership moved to another building on the compound that presented a lower profile and would have a greater chance of survival if we were hit by a plane.
“Notably, a decision was made that the personnel of the counter-terrorism center remained in the original headquarters building throughout that day … accepting the risk. The senior leadership team returned to the headquarters in the middle of the afternoon on 9/11.”
‘I had a briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was’
Some time afterwards, an order was given for the thousands of personnel in the building to evacuate. Some, including Henoch, were told to relocate to alternative sites to address the emergency.
But by the time of that instruction, nearby roads were choked with traffic as commuters returned home from Washington DC after being released from work early. That prevented agency staff from departing, and triggered fears that they could be sitting ducks for the doomed fourth plane, which was already known to be in the air.
“Large segments of the CIA operating staff were trapped,” Henoch said. “One guy, who was senior to me, was standing next to me in the car park and he said, ‘I have served in multiple war zones. I was a combat soldier in Vietnam and I’m going to die in the parking lot of the CIA.’”
The dysfunctional scene was soon replaced by one of much greater conviction – leading to permanent changes in US intelligence.
“I just remember loads of cable traffic coming in that said: it’s got to be al-Qaida,” said Henoch. “It wasn’t my world, so I had to have a quick briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was, because I just didn’t know anything about it.
“The change was immediate. The next morning, everybody at the Central Intelligence Agency had to know who they were, and how it intersected with everything you were doing.”
Steven Cash, a former CIA counter-terrorism officer who had left the agency to join the staff of the US Senate intelligence committee six months beforehand, faults the CIA’s pre-9/11 terrorism strategy as being too narrowly focused “looking to find bad guys” while neglecting the “political dimension”.
“There was an emphasis on looking at terrorists as if they were a motorcycle gang,” said Cash, who had specialized on the Lebanese Shia group Hezbollah, a close ally of Iran. “A decision was made in the first [George HW] Bush administration to take terrorism away from the people who looked at geographic areas and separate it out. [It was] illustrative of a mistaken way of looking at the world, because terrorists don’t exist in a vacuum.”
Cash moved on to focus on the Balkans before leaving the agency, but still harboured guilt after the attacks. “Was this our fault? Did we fail? That kind of guilt felt, at least for me, really personal.”
Cash had been on Capitol Hill, attending a committee meeting, when news of the attacks filtered through. “Somebody said, put on the TV and we saw the second plane hit,” he said. “And then they started evacuating the building.
“It was a mess. People were in the hall screaming, running around. The third plane had hit the Pentagon by that point, because we could see smoke across the National Mall.”
The following day, Cash and his then boss, the late Democratic senator Dianne Feinstein, visited CIA headquarters and found a mood of determined resolve. “It was all hands on deck. The people I knew were getting deployed very quickly to Afghanistan,” he recalled. “These people are pros. They didn’t care whether they were blamed or not. They wanted to do something.
“I have a little bit of survivor guilt here. Maybe I should have been shipped out to Afghanistan.”
Political pressure
On their visit to CIA headquarters on 12 September, senators asked agency operatives what legislation and resources they would need to respond to the attacks of the previous day, according to Cash.
Two early – and controversial – results were the USA Patriot Act of 2001, which expanded law enforcement and surveillance powers, and the Homeland Security Act of the following year, creating the US Department of Homeland Security, which houses agencies including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Later changes established the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, with the goal of coordinating 18 different intelligence bodies and eliminating the lack of coordination widely held to blame for warning signs of the 9/11 plot going unheeded.
“DNI was formed to make sure that we actually share everything with everybody. We don’t just keep it inside CIA,” said Susan Miller, a retired CIA counter-intelligence officer.
“What’s really cool is we’ve changed how we do things across the board, not just for terrorism. It’s really improved things. There was no coordination before.”
Yet the reaction to the attacks changed intelligence in another way – by making it more susceptible to political pressure, as President George W Bush’s administration searched for information that could be used to justify an invasion of Iraq to topple Saddam Hussein.
In September 2002, Henoch – who had previously studied Russian weapons capabilities working at the Stanford Research Institute – was asked to assess intelligence provided by an Iraqi defector codenamed Curveball, who had sought asylum in Germany, and provided its intelligence agency with what he said was proof of Saddam’s biological weapons program.
She quickly concluded the claims were fabricated, and passed her conclusions up the chain of command. They were not well received. When Colin Powell, the then US secretary of state, visited the CIA months later to review the agency’s intelligence on Iraq, Henoch and her fellow doubters were not informed. Powell’s subsequent speech to the United Nations security council in February 2003, in which he made the case for war, relied heavily on Curveball’s testimony – despite Henoch’s insistence when the address was checked with her and other officers beforehand that his assertions were not credible.
“We took a look at the Powell speech and I said: ‘You can’t use this. We think this is garbage,” she said. “I did write somewhere – I can’t remember on what page – ‘How can you send someone to die for something like this? No one ever answered that for me.
“The next thing I heard was, ‘Well, when we get in there, we’ll find something.’”
After the invasion, inspectors found no evidence of biological weapons. Curveball was later debunked as a fraud.
Miller, too, encountered the administration’s zeal for intelligence that could justify invading Iraq when she was posted to Prague as CIA station chief in 2002. Czech intelligence had investigated – and, initially, tentatively confirmed – a claim that one of the 9/11 ringleaders, Mohammed Atta, had travelled to Prague the previous year and met an Iraqi embassy official, Ahmad Samir al-Ani, months before the attacks.
The report was seized on by the hawkish US vice-president, Dick Cheney, as evidence of Saddam’s possible links to the attacks, thus providing another justification for war. But Czech intelligence officials retreated from their earlier stance, and the CIA concluded there was no evidence that the meeting happened.
Nevertheless, Donald Rumsfeld, then the US defense secretary, brazenly tried to revive it when Miller briefed him – along with George W Bush and Condoleezza Rice, the national security adviser – when they visited the Czech capital for a Nato summit in 2002.
“‘Young lady, you forgot about this other thing’,” Rumsfeld told Miller, she said. “I played dumb and said: ‘What other thing?’ He replied: ‘Mohammed Atta was here in Prague meeting the Iraqi consul.’
“Bush was looking really uncomfortable and Condi was looking straight ahead. I simply said, ‘Mr President, Madam Secretary, and Mr Rumsfeld, the CIA, the Czech service and I don’t make things up. We give you the facts, and the fact is that he was not here.’
“Bush and Rice nodded in acceptance and the ambassador supported me. But Rumsfeld threw his pen down in disgust.”
The invasion the neocons craved
Whether the supposed meeting happened or not, Rumsfeld and his neoconservative allies got the invasion they craved – leading to a protracted conflict that tarnished the CIA’s reputation and whose length, along with the coinciding US-led military campaign in Afghanistan, spurred popular opposition to “forever wars”.
Despite the blow to the agency’s standing, Cash insisted that its intelligence-gathering and functioning radically improved, thanks to the changes instituted after the attacks. “We have improved our intelligence capabilities significantly from what they were before 9/11,” he said, citing the success in preventing repeat attacks on US soil.
But with the Trump administration now engaged in a war with Iran, roiling the Middle East, such security could no longer be guaranteed, he believes.
“I’m not saying it was a great time,” Cash said, of the CIA’s record in the months and years after September 2001. “But the sense of purpose of being at a place in history where we – as a group, as a society – can do something, was pretty intoxicating.
“I was very proud to have been part of it. It sucked – but proud to have been part of it. And I think everything we’re seeing now is the antithesis of that.”

articles.title: Americans are seeking a pretext for another strike on Iran’s nuclear facilities
articles.body:
Americans are seeking a pretext for another strike on Iran’s nuclear facilities
In an interview with Hassan Hanizadeh, an international affairs expert, Shargh referred to the anti‑Iran resolution passed by the Board of Governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Hanizadeh said that this resolution was adopted under pressure from the United States and certain European countries to increase pressure on Iran and isolate it, and that its political dimension outweighs its technical aspects.
He stated that the resolution contains no new technical ambiguities that had not already been addressed, which indicates that Iran has taken the necessary steps toward transparency. Nevertheless, the Board of Governors and the IAEA Director General, in their reports on Iran’s nuclear activities, have focused primarily on political considerations and have ignored technical aspects. Referring this resolution to the UN Security Council could push Iran toward withdrawing from the Nuclear Non‑Proliferation Treaty (NPT)—although Russia and China may veto any resolution against Iran in the Security Council.
Iran: Let us not destroy our opportunities
The Iran newspaper spoke with Bahador Zarei, a professor of geopolitics, about Iran’s geographic and geopolitical capacities. Zarei said that although Iran is relatively small in geoeconomic terms, it is the 17th largest country in the world in terms of national power, national security, and territorial size. However, Iran is not strong in trade, with a trade volume of less than 50 billion dollars. Therefore, Iran must enter the global geoeconomic cycle and expand its commercial relations with various countries. In such a scenario, both the Caspian Sea in the north and the Persian Gulf in the south would gain strategic and geostrategic importance, enabling Iran to connect to Central Asia, the Caucasus, South Asia, West Asia, and Southwest Asia. Iran has land and maritime borders with 13 countries, which is one of the factors that makes Iran difficult to sanction effectively. If the issues surrounding the Strait of Hormuz are resolved, even if the United States seeks to impose sanctions on Iran, implementing such sanctions would not be easily feasible.
Siasat-e-Rooz: The US and Israel started the war, but Iran will end it
In its editorial, Siasat-e-Rooz focused on Iran’s regional power and its control over the Strait of Hormuz. The paper wrote that recent developments in the Persian Gulf and the US–Iran conflict show that the United States still imagines it can use its military and economic capacity to force Iran into submission and manage financial markets, hoping to reduce Trump’s economic challenges. In contrast, Iran—through new initiatives and by expanding the scope of its operations from the military domain into the technological, geopolitical, and economic spheres—is sending a clear message that control of the Strait of Hormuz remains in Iran’s hands. Ultimately, it is Tehran that determines the outcome of the war of endurance. The paper argues that no country can pass through the Strait of Hormuz or the Persian Gulf without Iran’s coordination and consent. This means that the United States and Israel may have initiated the conflict, but Iran will be the one to conclude it.
Jam-e-Jam: America’s attritional deadlock in the Strait of Hormuz
Jam-e Jam analyzed Iran’s powerful attacks on US positions in the region. According to the paper, the unprecedented damage suffered by the Pentagon and the CIA is the result of entirely flawed strategic decisions made by US policymakers in the war with Iran. The United States, by adopting an attritional strategy, has begun a new phase of continuous attacks on military infrastructure in the Strait of Hormuz. But these temporary successes have never been sustainable, as they are always met with immediate Iranian counter‑strikes, including drone attacks, while Iran’s industrial base remains intact. Applying this doctrine against a state actor exposes Washington to severe risks of miscalculation. While the US needs secure passage through the Strait, Iran can impose high costs simply by creating a sense of insecurity. This asymmetry, combined with the US inability to contain ballistic missile responses, has turned the conflict into a low‑intensity but persistent battle.
Hamshahri: The deterrence equation is on Iran’s table
Hamshahri analyzed Iran’s approach to the war with the United States, describing it as a war of equations—breaking existing equations and creating new ones. The paper argued that sustainable security has three pillars: deterrence, diplomacy aimed at reducing isolation, and national power and social cohesion. From this perspective, the Islamic Republic must maintain and strengthen deterrence, because weakening it would undermine the other two pillars and create serious risks and potential crises for the country. Deterrence has minimum and maximum levels. Iran has reached a certain level, but still has a long path ahead to reinforce it so that the very idea of attacking Iran becomes minimal.

articles.title: India Welcomes Russia, Iran Leaders for BRICS Summit Overshadowed by War
articles.body:
Leaders from Russia and Iran were in India for talks on Friday, ahead of a BRICS summit dominated by conflict and economic challenges, which Chinese President Xi Jinping will also attend.
Wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as global trade turbulence and oil are expected on the agenda at the two-day annual summit that opens on Saturday, when Xi is set to arrive.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It will be Xi’s first visit to India since 2019, and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Tibetan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
“China stands ready to work with India... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences,” Beijing’s foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said Friday.
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday -- exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 -- waving placards against Xi’s visit.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is due to hold talks on Friday with President Vladimir Putin, who last visited India in December 2025. Moscow is one of New Delhi’s most important strategic partners.
Russian Chemical Giant’s Plant in Perm Targeted in Ukrainian Drone Strike
“One should engage in debate and friendship only with the virtuous, and nothing whatsoever with the unvirtuous,” Modi wrote Friday, in a social media message in Sanskrit to welcome leaders to the 11-nation summit.
Posters of a beaming Modi line streets across New Delhi, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who arrived in New Delhi on Friday and will hold talks with Modi, said that “BRICS was established to counter unilateralism”, according to Tehran’s IRNA news agency.
- ‘Fault line’ -
As well as Iran, BRICS includes Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates -- countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.
All three have been admitted to the group in recent years, joining founding member states that include India, China and Russia.
“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit,” said Harsh V. Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation.
“What was seen until last year as an achievement -- the expansion of BRICS -- today looks like a big constraint on BRICS,” Pant said.
Pezeshkian’s participation -- his first visit to India as Iranian president -- will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
“The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the group’s cohesion,” said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is also expected, as is Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
New Delhi has navigated the energy crisis sparked by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia for fuel despite Western sanctions as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.

articles.title: Iran used AI to develop military, propaganda strategies, Anthropic report reveals
articles.body:
Iran repeatedly used American-made artificial intelligence systems to target US naval forces in the region, target Israeli and Jewish diaspora organizations, and develop phishing strategies inside the country, a Thursday Anthropic report revealed.
Anthropic described what it called an “Iran-nexus threat actor” that used Claude, the company’s flagship product, to develop targeting recommendations against US Navy targets.
The actor, according to Anthropic, used AI to identify and track naval positions and compile information, including “a roster of US personnel scraped from captions on public military photographs; publicly accessible ship and aircraft transponder identifiers; commercial satellite-imagery query scripts; and an inventory of public websites that exposed US naval movements.”
The unnamed organization also used AI to research vulnerabilities in shipboard systems, including “maritime VSAT terminals, Cisco communications equipment, and industrial control products,” according to the report.
This was one of the many findings revealed in the AI giant’s 154-page report, which delineated the dangers of US and Western adversaries such as Iran, China, and Russia utilizing the technology to pose security threats.
The report comes as debate over the dangers rages among policymakers and AI company employees, even as Anthropic refused the Pentagon’s February request to remove safety guardrails regarding mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons.
A Friday Wall Street Journal report revealed that a top researcher at Anthropic quit last week, citing fears that AI companies were developing uncontrollable systems.
'AI could kill all humans,' top Anthropic scientist says
Evan Hubinger, a top scientist at Anthropic, wrote in a social-media post, “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”
“I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” the WSJ cited him as saying.
Anthropic’s report revealed that all groups showed similar methodology. “They ran multi-victim campaigns using agentic AI that would previously have required teams of operators. They built custom tools, executed intrusions, and processed stolen data at volumes no individual human operator could manage manually,” the company explained.
In addition to targeting US military assets, Iran also developed an “automated, open-source intelligence identity-profiling harness” that targeted hundreds of Israeli governmental and non-governmental individuals, as well as Jewish diaspora organizations.
The actor used the system to collect and analyze open-source data, developing a pipeline that made malware harder to detect.
Iran using AI to survey, profile Iranians
Another two “Iranian nexus actors” used the company’s model to surveil and profile 6,388 Iranians in one year. The AI company claimed that Iran built an “analyst and production studio” used to run a social network analysis of over 155,216 tweets.
Among other domestic surveillance strategies were automatic license-plate recognition, mobile-device identifier interception, and private Telegram data analysis.
These operations targeted Iranian minorities, dissidents, and opponents of the Iranian regime abroad, according to the report.
Actors also used AI to run campaigns tied to “Jihad al-Tabyin,” or explanatory jihad, to produce propaganda in what they called a “soft war” or “cognitive warfare” program: a non-military plan to shape public opinion at home and abroad, the report explained.
Several Iranian organizations, including the Islamic Culture and Communications Organization (ICCO), were using AI to distribute Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) - aligned narratives, said the report.
The organizations used the technology to build operational manuals, create persona systems, develop content strategies, and transform official government material into targeted messaging.
Yemeni group developing missiles with AI
Anthropic also claimed that a northern-Yemeni group was using Claude to develop guidance software for high-end weapons, including a multi-stage ballistic missile.
This comes as the Iranian-backed Houthis consolidate control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. Anthropic said that its safeguards had blocked many of the group’s requests to develop the weapons, “but not all of them.”
The company confirmed that it had taken the necessary steps to ban the account, develop detections to prevent future use, and share intelligence with government authorities.
“We hope that the findings in this report will help other developers recognize similar patterns on their own platforms, give governments and civil society a clearer view of how emerging threats take shape, and strengthen collective defenses,” it said.

articles.title: Ukraine hits key Russia-Iran logistics hub in Caspian Sea, damages three Russian warships
articles.body:
Ukraine says its forces struck Russia’s Makhachkala port on the Caspian Sea and confirmed damage to three Russian warships in the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in a series of long-range attacks.
Ukraine’s General Staff said the Makhachkala Sea Commercial Port in Russia’s Dagestan was hit overnight on 10 September, with a fire recorded at the site. The extent of the damage is still being assessed.
The Special Operations Forces (SSO) said Ukrainian units struck oil infrastructure at the port in a joint operation with other Defense Forces. The port’s oil terminal handles tankers with a capacity of up to 10,000 tonnes, while an oil depot is located nearby, according to the SSO.
Makhachkala is Russia’s only ice-free deepwater port on the Caspian Sea and operates year-round. The General Staff said it is an important link in the Russia-Iran logistics corridor, which Moscow uses to bypass Western sanctions.
According to the General Staff, the route is used to transport military-related cargo in both directions, including components and Shahed-type attack drones from Iran to Russia, and explosives, drone components, and ammunition from Russia to Iran. A base of Russia’s Caspian Flotilla is also located near the port.
The SSO said damaging the port’s oil infrastructure could reduce Russia’s ability to use the Caspian Sea to transport and transship energy resources.
Fire Point, a Ukrainian drone manufacturer, said Ukrainian forces used its FP-1 drones in the attack. The company said Makhachkala had been used as a transit point for Iranian attack drones delivered to Russia by sea before being moved onward for use against Ukraine.
Fire Point also said the port handled more than 2.9 million tonnes of cargo in the first eight months of 2026, including more than 2.08 million tonnes of oil.
Three Russian warships hit in Novorossiysk
Ukraine’s General Staff also said further analysis of data confirmed damage inflicted on three Russian warships in the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk on 9 September, along with fuel-oil storage facilities at the port.
The General Staff identified the vessels as the small sea minesweeper Zheleznyakov, the frigate Admiral Essen, and the Project 11711 landing ship Pyotr Morgunov.
Visual analysis published by Exilenova+ reported strikes on another Russian warship, the Buyan-M-class corvette, as well as confirming strikes on the frigates Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov. The outlet said the Essen was hit in its superstructure and caught fire.
The Buyan-M class is capable of carrying Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. Russia has used such ships to launch strikes against Ukraine.
The Ukrainian General Staff said operations against key Russian military targets are continuing.

articles.title: GA-ASI’s Uncrewed Combat Aviation Portfolio Answers Call for High-End Warfare Capability
articles.body:
General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Inc. (GA-ASI), the company that introduced the world to unmanned warfare, has systematically transformed its aircraft lineup to address the defining requirements of modern high-technology warfare: range, persistence, payload, survivability, and scale against advanced adversaries.
The portfolio now spans from the company’s enhanced MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian platforms capable of long-range maritime strike, to the expeditionary Mojave STOL, to the Air Force’s newly selected FQ-42A Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) — its first uncrewed fighter — and, most recently, to the Wildfire Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA), a theater-range platform engineered for affordable, attrition-tolerant combat mass.
According to GA-ASI President David Alexander, the United States has entered an era where winning demands large, capable Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (UAS) that can operate from friendly airspace into contested environments affordably, without risking aircrews.
“We’ve never been a company that rested on its laurels,” said Alexander. “The conversation around uncrewed systems has changed, and frankly, it should. The battlefield has evolved, threats have evolved, and so have we.
“We’re keeping ahead of the game, and, in the case of our FQ-42A and Wildfire aircraft, we’ve designed them from the start to overmatch threats today and into the future.”
Physics Demands Large Airframes
Losses in contested environments have prompted some observers to suggest moving away from large UAS platforms. Alexander sees those same operations as validation for continued investment in evolved large UAS.
“Yes, we’ve seen combat losses,” he said. “We’ve also heard Pentagon leaders call our Reaper the ‘MVP’ of the campaign. That tells you something important. When a system consistently delivers decisive effects, you modernize it and build on it. And I believe that’s where the Department of War is headed.”
Alexander emphasized that Reaper was purpose-built to provide persistent surveillance, long endurance, and precision strike. MQ-9A delivers these capabilities at scale and at a fraction of the cost of manned platforms that put pilots’ lives at risk, he added.
The proliferation of small drones — quadcopters, gliders, and short-range rockets — doesn’t change fundamental operational requirements, he said.
Despite the hype, smaller platforms “can’t change physics,” Alexander noted.
“Long-range, high-payload, high-endurance missions require large, hefty airframes with significant wingspan, fuel capacity, and payload volume,” he continued. “If we are serious about surveilling and targeting across wide ocean areas, tracking mobile missile units, and holding adversary assets at risk from standoff distances, large UAS modernized for contested environments are the decisive advantage.”
Wildfire: Delivering Attritable Mass at Theater Range
Wildfire represents GA-ASI’s answer to a critical requirement: affordable combat mass that can sustain losses while maintaining operational pressure across contested theaters.
This theater-range, high-production UAS is designed specifically for high-threat environments:
Combat payload and range: Wildfire can carry two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles (LRASM) or four Joint Strike Missiles (JSM) for meaningful combat distances and has a ferry range that exceeds 8,000 nautical miles. This enables delivery of weapons, sensors, electronic warfare capabilities, or communications relay deep into contested battlespace.
Modular architecture: Open interfaces and modular payload hard points enable modularity to support rapid mission reconfiguration, allowing commanders to adapt as threats and priorities shift during operations.
Volume production: Leveraging more than 5 million square feet of manufacturing capacity and advanced production processes, Wildfire is engineered to be built and fielded in numbers sufficient to absorb attrition while maintaining persistent theater-wide pressure.
Combined with Gambit Series capabilities, Wildfire delivers what defense leaders call “attritable mass”— large numbers of capable systems whose loss does not constitute strategic setback because they are affordable, uncrewed, and replaceable.
Gambit Series: Autonomous Combat Jets for Peer Threats
The Gambit Series represents GA-ASI’s family of autonomous jets for high-end contested operations. Built around a common core comprising roughly 70 percent of key components, the platform’s modular architecture drives down costs while simplifying production, logistics, and sustainment.
Recently selected by the U.S. Air Force for its CCA program, the FQ-42A — designed to fly alongside fighters like the F-22 — is a variant of GA-ASI’s Gambit 2.
Across six missionized Gambit variants, the architecture supports:
- Long-endurance ISR in contested airspace
- Air-to-air combat
- Adversary training for advanced threat replication
- Stealth reconnaissance in denied areas
- Carrier-based naval operations
- Penetrating air-to-ground strike and suppression of enemy air defenses
All Gambit aircraft are designed for human-machine teaming with advanced fighters and other UAS, extending sensors, adding weapons capacity, and imposing complex targeting dilemmas on adversary defenses — precisely the type of effects envisioned in modern Air Force operational concepts.
Mojave STOL: Airpower, Hold the Tarmac
Built on GA-ASI’s other pioneering aircraft, Mojave STOL addresses a critical vulnerability in modern combat: dependence on large runways.
Short Takeoff and Landing (STOL) capability: Mojave STOL operates from austere, unprepared locations — open fields, dry riverbeds, even amphibious assault ship decks — generating uncrewed combat airpower from sites adversaries cannot easily target or predict.
Advanced sensor integration: Controllable via human-portable, laptop-based ground control systems, Mojave STOL carries cutting-edge radar, electro-optical/infrared, and signals intelligence payloads, providing a comprehensive operational picture for precise targeting and situational awareness to support dispersed forces.
In a combat environment where large runways are vulnerable to adversary strikes, Mojave STOL establishes airfields without airports. Its rugged construction enables persistent ISR and strike capability sourced from improvised mobile launch and recovery sites.
MQ-9B: Evolved Flagship Platform for Standoff Operations
MQ-9B SkyGuardian and SeaGuardian remain GA-ASI’s flagship multi-mission ISR platforms, now upgraded for long-range contested operations and integration into distributed kill chains.
Long-range weapons integration: New pylons with 30-inch lug spacing accommodate larger standoff munitions, including LRASM and JSM. Combined with MQ-9B’s advanced ISR suite, this transforms the aircraft into a long-range strike and maritime interdiction platform capable of engaging far outside adversary standoff ranges.
Resilient communications: Integration with proliferated Low Earth Orbit (pLEO) satellite constellations provides low-latency, high-bandwidth, jam-resistant connectivity. In combination with DoD-standard cybersecurity, MQ-9B maintains secure command-and-control and sensor links globally, even under electronic attack.
For Air Force and joint planners, MQ-9B has evolved beyond counterinsurgency roots into a standoff sensor-shooter that functions as a resilient node in distributed operations.
Urgency Driven by Evolving Threats
Alexander noted that changing battlefield conditions have continually driven the company to advance its technology and operational concepts.
“When you look at the threats we’re seeing in Ukraine and Iran, we already knew our aircraft would need to evolve, and we’ve been pushing ahead there for years now,” he said. “But it seems like every morning the news puts fresh urgency behind delivering that vital combat capability while finding ways to strip out some of what drives up costs.”
That urgency is backed by unmatched operational experience. To date, GA-ASI has accumulated nearly 10 million flight hours, the vast majority in combat operations.
Taken as a whole, Alexander said, the aircraft portfolio shows that GA-ASI is serious about retaining its position as the leading provider of UAS to the United States and its allies.
“We know, to our core, what it takes to deliver relevant systems,” he said. “We have the people, infrastructure, and capacity in place, today, to do it at scale.
“GA-ASI is ready to answer the call.”

articles.title: Anthropic details bad actors’ efforts to misuse its AI for bioweapons
articles.body:
Criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have attempted to use Anthropic’s powerful artificial intelligence models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents, according to a threat intelligence report the company published on Thursday.
“The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,” Anthropic wrote in its 154-page report. “We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services.”
In particular, the company detailed five case studies of scientists using its AI models in biological research. In these examples, Anthropic said the researchers circumvented its safeguards meant to prevent users from “unsupported regions”, as well as worked to hide the purpose of their work.
“Biological misuse is one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models,” Anthropic wrote. “Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities could have catastrophic consequences.”
Anthropic said it banned these accounts. The company did not reveal the names of the research institutions or the countries where the misuse took place, saying it was uncertain of the researchers’ intent.
Anthropic gave dozens of other examples of threat actors using its AI models. Those included cyber operations such as Russian espionage and “smash-and-grab” cyberhacks; surveillance operations, including a China-based program targeting Uyghurs in Syria and another targeting internal dissidents; propaganda campaigns in Russia, Malaysia, Iran and Bangladesh; and the use of its Claude AI model in Yemen, China and Russia to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs and other munitions.
In one of the examples of biological research, Anthropic found a scientist using Claude to work on a state-sponsored grant application to study the virus chikungunya. The virus is a mosquito-borne disease, similar to dengue and malaria, that can cause months of severe pain, fever and other debilitating symptoms.
Such research could be used to develop vaccines, but could also be used to create biological weapons. Anthropic told the New York Times this case was especially concerning because it could see the study was to be done at a military research institute.
The report comes just two days after an Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, set off a media firestorm with his resignation. He stated that he quit the company because it was not acting responsibly in creating its technology. Coxon said Anthropic and its rival, OpenAI, were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence” that would cause human extinction by 2030. Current Anthropic employees posted public agreements with him.
Many AI experts say the real-world threats, like those detailed in Anthropic’s intelligence report, are far more concerning within the next three years than an apocalypse brought on by an omnipotent intelligence.
“AI accelerationism and AI doomerism are two sides of the same coin: they both enforce the notion that an AGI superbeing will come into existence,” said Heidy Khlaaf, the chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute. Khlaaf said AI labs creating technology that can be used for cybersecurity exploitation and weapons of war could be exceedingly more deadly.
In its report, Anthropic said that the potential real-world misuse from AI models is not typically in public view, instead, it’s investigated internally and by academics, governments and international organizations.
The company said that the entire AI industry needs to work together, alongside governments, to address these harms and create defenses.
“As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer,” Anthropic wrote.

articles.title: Money, not engineering, is what stands between Ukraine and Russia’s fastest drones, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Ukraine has not had enough of the right weapons to shoot down Russia's jet-powered drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at a press conference with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Calgary on 10 September. He put the remaining obstacles at time and money rather than engineering, and used the appearance to press partners for joint production. Russia attacks Ukrainian cities with drones every night, and the defense against the fastest of them is still being built.
"We did not have enough means"
Zelenskyy was answering a question about the Russian drone found at Leipzig airport in Germany and the drone that delayed his own flight out of Moldova.
"We have to be very frank: we did not have enough means to destroy all these fast drones," he said. "Yes, we are on the way, more than 60 companies are already working on this. Yes, we will get a result, but it takes time."
Three days earlier, he noted that only three to five of the firms show real results.
Germany blames Moscow for Leipzig drone attack, closes consulate and cultural center among sweeping diplomatic measures
The bottleneck is money
He then went past the engineering.The problem is not only technology, he said, but the funding to build thousands of interceptors every single day.
That arithmetic sends Ukraine abroad with its blueprints.
"That is why we talk about joint production, about production lines in one country or another," Zelenskyy said.
Russia now builds about 3,000 jet-powered drones a month, by Ukrainian military intelligence's count, and fired some 800 of them in four days at the end of August. They fly faster than propeller Shaheds and are harder to bring down, which has stretched air raid alerts nationwide. Ukraine's Air Force cannot yet rely on usual interceptor drones against them.
One drone, of the kind that turned up at Leipzig or crossed Moldova, is not a problem for Ukraine, Zelenskyy said. Thousands of fast drones a day are.
One Russian drone held up seven flights in Moldova, Zelenskyy’s trip to Norway for King Harald V’s funeral among them
What a night without enough interceptors looks like
The same night, Russia sent 161 long-range attack drones at Ukraine, decoys among them, along with a cruise missile.That is an ordinary night now, and its damage spreads thin across the map instead of landing in one place.
A Russian strike set a nine-story apartment block alight in Kyiv, burning the facade up to the fifth floor and a flat on the second. Firefighters carried seven people out and handed seven more to medics. Russian drones injured eight people in the capital overnight.
North of the city, Russia burned warehouses in the Bucha district, then struck the same site again while the crews were still dousing the flames.
In Dnipro, the drones kept coming back, more than ten times from the evening on, damaging a plant and a row of garages and injuring seven people.
Farther out, Russia injured a mother and her son in Zaporizhzhia and damaged a plant in Zhytomyr Oblast, and the waves ran west far enough that NATO jets went up over Romania.

articles.title: Iranian strikes force UAE to dismantle plans for its AI mega-campus
articles.body:
Iranian strikes force UAE to dismantle plans for its AI mega-campus
TEHRAN — The United Arab Emirates is quietly dismantling its blueprint for a 5-gigawatt artificial intelligence project, abandoning plans for a centralized campus in Abu Dhabi in favor of a dispersed network of hardened facilities.
Iranian missile and drone operations have permanently altered the security calculus for regional autocracies hosting American forces.
Originally envisioned as a 10-square-mile computing hub built in partnership with U.S. tech firms, the project is undergoing a total strategic redesign.
According to a Reuters report on September 11, 2026, Emirati officials are now calculating the financial burden of moving sensitive infrastructure underground into the rugged mountain ranges of Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah, equipping dispersed sites with blast-resistant concrete and electronic jamming apparatus.
Retaliation shatters the safe haven myth
The sudden overhaul follows retaliatory strikes by Iranian forces targeting infrastructure linked to foreign military presence across the region.
In March, drone strikes damaged two Amazon Web Services data centers in the UAE alongside a major facility in Bahrain, triggering prolonged disruptions across regional cloud networks and banking systems.
The impact demonstrated how quickly commercial digital infrastructure collapses when tied to Western military footprint.
Pressure intensified in April when Iran’s armed forces released targeting footage explicitly identifying Stargate UAE, the project’s $30 billion first phase.
The video confirmed the exact coordinates of the site adjacent to Al Dhafra Air Base, an enclave housing U.S. troops that has been targeted repeatedly since the wider war began in February.
The cost of subservience
The flagship project was built on a geopolitical bargain. Spearheaded by G42, an entity controlled by Emirati national security adviser Tahnoun bin Zayed, Abu Dhabi agreed to sever technological ties with China in exchange for advanced Nvidia microprocessors and infrastructure deals with American corporations such as OpenAI, Oracle, and Cisco.
By embedding critical digital infrastructure next to active launchpads for U.S. military operations, Abu Dhabi tied its economic future directly to Washington’s regional warfare.
When the U.S. and Israel launched their campaign of aggression against Iran, the UAE’s decision to host and abet hostile forces, provide basing and logistics for operations against Iran, and make itself complicit in Washington’s anti-Iran bloc transformed its high-tech megaprojects into vulnerable targets.
Scattered infrastructure and mounting financial costs
Emirati planners are now scrambling to break the 5-gigawatt masterplan into fragmented sites across multiple emirates.
Workloads handling military and government data will be buried inside disused mines and subterranean mountain vaults.
Planners are also integrating localized missile interceptors, blast walls, and redundant power networks to survive potential strikes.
These physical modifications carry immense financial and logistical burdens. Splitting a unified mega-campus into isolated, blast-proof facilities multiplies energy consumption, physical security perimeters, and specialized cooling requirements at every single site.
While G42 and its Western partners claim the build proceeds as planned, the physical reality tells a different story.
Abu Dhabi traded its national sovereignty for American hardware and military promises, only to discover that no Western air defense shield can protect infrastructure erected in the shadow of U.S. military bases.

articles.title: Turkish combat drone gets a longer-range strike weapon
articles.body:
- Baykar has integrated Roketsan's new 300-ER air-launched ballistic missile onto its Akıncı combat drone, with a test launch expected soon.
- The missile can strike targets more than 500 km away and extends a family of shorter-range weapons already fired from the Akıncı.
Turkish drone maker Baykar has fitted its Akıncı unmanned combat aircraft with Roketsan’s new 300-ER air-launched ballistic missile, with a first launch from the drone expected soon, according to Ulusavunma.
Roketsan first showed the 300-ER publicly at the IDEF defense show in Istanbul in July 2025, presenting it as the longest-range weapon yet in a family of air-launched missiles that began with the shorter İHA-122 and İHA-230. The missile can hit targets more than 500 km (310 miles) away, depending on the altitude it is launched from.
The 300-ER measures about 5 meters (16 feet) long, weighs 900 kg (1,980 lb) and carries a warhead of more than 150 kg (330 lb) inside a 370 mm-diameter body. It navigates using GNSS and inertial guidance and switches to a TV camera seeker for the final approach to the target, a setup Roketsan says is built for precision strikes on radars, armored vehicles, air defense systems and command centers.
The missile extends a lineage Roketsan built from its ground-launched artillery rockets. The company adapted its 122 mm and 230 mm-class rockets into the air-launched İHA-122 and İHA-230, both of which Baykar has already test-fired from the Akıncı, hitting targets roughly 55 km and 100 km away in past trials. The 300-ER carries that same approach out to a much longer range, inside a larger airframe.
That range matters because it lets a large drone like the Akıncı release a weapon and turn away before coming within reach of many surface-to-air missile systems built to intercept aircraft rather than incoming ballistic threats. Roketsan has said the missile is also intended for use on fighter jets and on Baykar’s jet-powered Kızılelma combat drone.
Roketsan told Turkish media in April 2026 that it expected to complete initial test firings of the 300-ER and deliver the missile to the Turkish Armed Forces within the year. Baykar’s September 10 statement does not say whether that test launch has already taken place or specify a date for it, and neither company has disclosed when the missile might enter regular service.

articles.title: “Credit to the Russians, they know how to scale,” Ukrainian military spokesperson says. Ukraine’s jet-drone interceptors show early promise, but harder job ahead
articles.body:
Ukraine is getting closer to home-built interceptors designed to hunt down Russia's fast jet Gerans. Those interceptors have shown very positive early results, and the harder job now is producing enough of them to match the speed at which Ukraine downs the slower drones, Serhii Bratchuk, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Volunteer Army, said on Radio NV.
The jet-powered Geran is the problem Ukraine has been racing to solve. It flies too fast for the mobile gun teams and light interceptors that bring down the slower, piston-engine version. Alongside ballistic missiles, those drones have already done strategic damage: they helped Russia destroy about 90 percent of Ukraine's modern warehouse capacity.
A working interceptor changes that only if Ukraine can field it in numbers, which is why Bratchuk framed the fight ahead as one of production rather than invention.
Interceptors show early promise
However, Bratchuk would not put a date on their release, saying that "right now, our developers are testing our jet interceptor drones."
"We can't talk about details, but from what I know and what I see, the results are very positive, and we are counting on them," he shared.
Four Ukrainian companies already have interceptor drones in field trials, and President Zelenskyy has said that 67 firms in all are working to shoot down the jet drones en masse.
Production must catch up
Ukraine has to lift jet-drone interception to the level it has reached against the conventional Gerans, Bratchuk said, the ones Ukrainians nickname "mopeds" for their buzzing engines. Only then, he argued, can Ukraine say it is closing the sky to the fast drones as it has to the slow ones.
Russia keeps firing both types, in the south and elsewhere, and often at night, precisely to overload Ukraine's air defenses.
Russia scales, and Ukraine must too
Bratchuk gave Russia its due on the one thing that will decide this contest, its ability to turn out weapons in volume.
"Credit to the Russians. They know how to scale," he said.
Ukraine has to learn the same lesson, he argued, and he believes it can, having pulled off fast build-ups before.
"There are examples where we really do learn fast and scale up the relevant processes. So when it comes to jet interceptor drones, we very much want that scaling," he added.

articles.title: Ukraine and Canada Sign 100-Year Partnership and Drone Deal
articles.body:
Ukraine and Canada signed a Declaration on 100-Year Partnership, which provides for expanding cooperation to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership.
This became known following the meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Calgary, the Office of the latter reported.
As part of the agreements, the states are launching their first deal on unmanned systems (Drone Deal) with a country in the Americas.
In Alberta, the leaders inspected drone models that will be the first to be deployed as part of this defense initiative.
The agreement provides for Canada to order large quantities of drones, with 30% of the manufactured equipment to be supplied to Ukraine.
The parties expressed their intention to establish a long-term defense-industrial partnership for the joint production of unmanned systems, counter-drone systems, and electronic warfare systems.
In addition, the Canadian side confirmed a new military aid package aimed at strengthening Ukraine’s air defense.
Canada will focus on supplying the necessary air defense systems and interceptor missiles, while continuing to provide ammunition and military equipment.
The partners extended the Operation UNIFIER training mission to prepare Ukrainian service members through 2029.
Both countries will deepen cooperation in intelligence, cyber defense, countering hybrid threats and foreign information manipulation.
It is worth recalling that on January 16, Volodymyr Zelensky and former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer signed an agreement on a century-long partnership between the two countries.
During a joint press conference, the President of Ukraine announced an agreement on continued annual military assistance and an expansion of the training program for Ukrainian troops.

articles.title: Putin and Xi in India for BRICS summit as Ukraine, Middle East wars loom
articles.body:
Putin arrives in India for BRICS summit set to be dominated by Middle East, Ukraine wars
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in New Delhi on Friday for a two-day BRICS summit expected to focus on wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and economic challenges. Putin and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian are due to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while China’s Xi Jinping is also expected to hold talks.
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in the Indian capital on Friday ahead of an 11-member BRICS summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.
Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian were due to hold talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while Chinese President Xi Jinping was also expected to meet him on the sidelines of the two-day meeting, according to Indian diplomatic sources.
Putin arrived at Palam Air Force Station in New Delhi, where he was greeted by India's Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia's Ria Novosti news agency.
For China's Xi, it will be his first visit to India since 2019 and marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
Read moreChina, Russia conclude BRICS+ naval drills in South Africa amid controversy
'Fault line'
Posters of a beaming Modi line streets across New Delhi to welcome leaders, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
It has since expanded and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.
"The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit," said Harsh V. Pant of India's Observer Research Foundation.
"What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of BRICS – today looks like a big constraint on BRICS," Pant said.
Read moreXi calls on Mideast nations to be ‘masters of their own affairs’ in rare Egypt visit
It will be Pezeshkian's first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
"The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the (expanded) group's cohesion," said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Putin last visited India in December 2025, but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was "grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Russia has fired its Oreshnik with six warheads at Ukraine three times. State Duma defense committee member says “hour is not far” before fourth one
articles.body:
A member of Russia's parliament has threatened a fresh strike on Ukraine with the Oreshnik, Russia's intermediate-range ballistic missile. Andrei Kolesnik, of the State Duma's defense committee, says the "hour is not far" when Ukraine will "feel what Oreshnik is," casting the strike as revenge for a Ukrainian attack on the Russian city of Sochi, Russian state media reported, according to UNIAN.
Russia has already fired the Oreshnik at Ukraine three times, starting with Dnipro in November 2024, then the Lviv Oblast in January, a strike that landed roughly 70 kilometers from the Polish border and NATO's edge, and again near Bila Tserkva in Kyiv Oblast in May.
Kolesnik frames a strike as revenge
Kolesnik cast the coming strike as an answer to what he called Ukrainian terrorism against civilians. He pointed to a recent Ukrainian attack on Sochi, noting that Ukraine's forces used unmanned naval boats rather than drones.
"This is a terrorist attack in its purest form," he said, adding, "I think the hour is not far when the Ukrainian side will feel what Oreshnik is."
But what Kolesnik did not mention in his threats is that Russia hits Ukraine daily. Kyiv has been under a constant attack by jet-powered drones that trigger an air alert almost hourly since 27 August. Russia also fires presumably two ballistic missile attacks on the Ukrainian capital two times a week, inflicting $12 million in damages per strike and killing civilians. Meanwhile, other regions come under Russian attacks with the same intensity and suffer from Russian advances in the east and south of Ukraine.
The missile is a message more than a weapon
The Oreshnik carries six warheads and flies at around Mach 11. All three strikes were launched from the Kapustin Yar range in southern Russia, according to Ukraine's air force.
Russia has kept up that pressure by deploying a missile brigade to Belarus, positioning that would put more of Europe within the missile's reach.

articles.title: ‘Go home, man. You’re embarrassing.’ U.S. officials are reportedly eager for the CIA director to take over Russia–Ukraine talks from Witkoff.
articles.body:
‘Go home, man. You’re embarrassing.’ U.S. officials are reportedly eager for the CIA director to take over Russia–Ukraine talks from Witkoff.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s potential emergence as Washington’s chief negotiator on the Russia–Ukraine war has energized many U.S. officials, even though the White House has officially denied any such plan, Politico reported.
The Financial Times wrote on September 9 that Ratcliffe would take on a “larger role” representing the United States in the negotiations. American officials had shared that information with their European counterparts, according to the paper.
Steve Witkoff would continue participating in the negotiations alongside Ratcliffe, the FT wrote, while Jared Kushner could shift his focus to settling the war in Gaza and the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. The White House press office called the Financial Times report “totally fake news.”
Politico’s sources describe Ratcliffe as a stronger negotiator than Witkoff. But one of them stressed that simply replacing the special envoy won’t be enough to change the situation: nothing will shift until the United States starts putting real pressure on Russia through tougher sanctions and increased military aid to Ukraine.
“If Ratcliffe gets involved, he knows Russian issues very well,” Matthew Boyse, who worked on Eurasian affairs at the State Department during the first Trump administration, told the outlet. He also cautioned against expecting quick success in negotiations under Ratcliffe, since Vladimir Putin believes time is on his side and therefore “is showing no interest in moving off fixed maximalist positions.”
Many in Washington also welcome Ratcliffe’s potential appointment, viewing Witkoff’s approach as amateurish. After a recent meeting with Putin, for instance, Witkoff said: “When we retire, we’ll have all these incredible stories and incredible memories, and yours will be right at the top of it all.” An unnamed Washington official responded: “Who talks about retirement in literally one of the most critical meetings, ever? Go home man, you’re embarrassing.”
A Politico source in Ukraine said they had no information yet indicating Ratcliffe would take charge of the Russia–Ukraine issue but stressed that Kyiv has been “working with the U.S. at every level, including the CIA.”
Ratcliffe flew to Moscow in late August, though the purpose of the trip remains unclear. Officials in both the United States and Russia downplayed its significance, describing it as a routine visit within the framework of intelligence agency contacts. Western media outlets have offered widely differing accounts of the trip’s real purpose, ranging from a call to scale back cooperation with Iran to a warning against attacking NATO countries.

articles.body:
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian defense-industry plant producing components for military aircraft engines, along with air defense systems, a radar station and drone facilities, the AFU General Staff said on Friday, Sept. 11.
The strikes hit Russian military targets in several regions and occupied Ukrainian territories, according to Ukraine’s military.

The most significant target was the Snizhne Machine-Building Plant in the occupied Donetsk region. The facility produces components for gas-turbine engines, including compressor and turbine blades, and supplies parts used in Russian military aviation.
Ukrainian forces also targeted two Pantsir-S1 air defense systems in Taganrog, Rostov Oblast, a Russian radar station in Berezki, Bryansk Oblast, and a facility in Donetsk used to store, prepare and launch attack drones.
In the occupied Luhansk region, Ukrainian forces struck an FPV drone operator training center and a unit of the Chechen Akhmat forces in Petropavlivka.
The General Staff did not provide details on the extent of damage at the targeted sites, saying the results were still being assessed.
The strikes are part of Ukraine’s ongoing campaign against Russian military infrastructure and the defense-industrial network supporting Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Part of wider Ukrainian drone campaign
The reported attack came amid a broader wave of overnight Ukrainian drone strikes against Russian industrial infrastructure.

In Perm, a major chemical plant was reportedly targeted by Ukrainian drones early Friday, Sept. 11, with footage appearing to show a drone diving toward the facility.
In Saratov, a fire was reported at the Rosneft-owned Saratov Oil Refinery, while an Ozon logistics center also reportedly caught fire.
In Volgograd, regional authorities reported damage to an industrial facility and an apartment building, with two people hospitalized.
Ozon logistics hubs have increasingly been targeted since late August. Seven warehouses have reportedly been hit across Samara, Rostov, and Belgorod oblasts, Krasnodar Krai, Bashkortostan, and Dagestan.
The attacks also come as Ukraine continues to target Russia’s oil-refining sector. Ukrainian drones have struck Russian refineries at least 70 times since the beginning of 2026, according to Bloomberg, contributing to a sharp decline in refining output and growing gasoline shortages.
At least 17 Russian regions have introduced restrictions on fuel sales, while Russia has increasingly turned to imports from India, Morocco, Turkey, and Belarus to cover the shortfall.
The Russian defense ministry had not released a tally of intercepted drones from the latest wave, while Ukraine had not officially claimed responsibility for the reported attacks.

Approximately 25,000 North Korean troops have already rotated through the Russian armed forces, Lieutenant General Oleh Ivaschenko, Chief of the Main Intelligence Agency (GUR) of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, said in an interview with The Times.

articles.title: How the U.S. Treasury's New Aviation Sanctions on Iran Extend Beyond Tehran
articles.body:
The U.S. Treasury issued sweeping new sanctions against Iran on Tuesday, targeting the country’s airlines and their international service providers as it ramps up its effort to isolate Tehran from the global economy.
The aviation sanctions form a significant part of the Trump Administration's ”Operation Economic Outcast,” which the White House has described as “an unprecedented campaign to sever every remaining economic lifeline sustaining the Islamic Republic of Iran.” As negotiations have stalled, and with the U.S. and Iran engaged in active hostilities once more, the economic pressure is intended to push Tehran into a deal to end the war.
The U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned 27 Iranian airlines, accusing them of having “long supported the Iranian regime’s destabilizing activities.” The sweeping measures were largely focused on grounding Mahan Air, which was first sanctioned by the U.S. in 2011 and is also subject to E.U. sanctions. The carrier has long been accused of transporting personnel, equipment, and funds for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC).
The measures build on OFAC’s April and July actions “targeting persons servicing Mahan Air’s domestic and international flights,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
The U.S. also designated firms based outside of Iran that it said had helped Mahan Air maintain operations by providing goods or services. This action specifically targets “covert front companies, foreign intermediaries, and deceptive transshipment routes that Iran relies on to obtain U.S.-origin aircraft and sensitive technology,” according to the Treasury.
The OFAC also suspended three Iran-related aviation authorizations that “allowed for overflights, and for non-U.S. airlines to fly U.S.-origin or U.S.-controlled commercial aircraft into Iran.”
The sanctions, and their international reach, are intended to "intensify Iran's economic isolation, to further degrade their military capability, and push them to some kind of a concession or settlement that favors the United States,” Jack Roush, a PhD candidate affiliated with the Iranian History Initiative at the London School of Economics, tells TIME.
Here’s what to know about the latest sanctions, how they extend beyond the borders of Iran, and the economic pressure mounting against Tehran.
Aviation sanctions target Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Turkey, and UAE-based firms
The U.S. Treasury has accused Iran of using front companies and other pass-through entities in third countries in an attempt to evade aviation links back to Tehran and has extended sanctions to nine internationally-based entities it alleges have aided these efforts.
Measures were imposed on two UAE-based commercial entities and a UAE-based individual, as well as one Turkish-based and one U.K.-based firm.
Four cargo providers and general sales agents were also sanctioned, accused of servicing Mahan Air and coordinating shipments on behalf of the airline. Two are based in Turkey, one in Kazakhstan, and one in Malaysia.
The new sweeping sanctions “will exacerbate challenges that Iran already faces in maintaining its fleet,” says Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at Chatham House.
With the reliance on foreign entities to maintain Iran’s aging fleet, the measures targeting companies outside of Iran will likely damage Tehran’s aviation capabilities, she says, as it will “restrict Iran's ability to rely on those regional hubs” and could prompt “international carriers [to] further reduce or suspend Iranian services.”
“If that happens, then this becomes a blockade of Iran's aviation infrastructure, which is quite serious,” says Vakil.
U.S. issues warning to anyone doing business with Iran amid effort to choke Tehran off from global economy
The U.S. Treasury has vowed to isolate any international entity that continues to show support to Mahan Air. “Let this be a warning to anyone doing business with Iran’s remaining airlines, all of which we sanctioned,” Bessent said. “You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system.”
In recent weeks, the U.S. has imposed sanctions on banking institutions in other countries, accusing the lenders of enabling Iran.
On. Aug. 28, the U.S. moved to cut off Egyptian Banque Misr's UAE-located branches from the dollar-based financial system. Banque Misr said it is reviewing the notice from the U.S. Treasury and will communicate with the department “to obtain further information and maintain ongoing cooperation.”
Days later, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned Turkey's Golden Global investment bank and two subsidiaries, accusing it of enabling the transfer of oil revenues from China to Iran. Golden Global rejected the allegations, calling them “entirely unfounded and inconsistent.”
The sanctions were significant, marking the first time a bank in a NATO ally had been hit under the current economic campaign, experts told Reuters.
These recent U.S. sanctions on Turkish firms are the latest points of tension between the two countries. In 2019, Turkish state-run lender Halkbank was charged in a Manhattan federal court, accused of participating in a “multibillion-dollar Iranian sanctions evasion scheme.”
The charges—referred to by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan as “ugly”—dragged on for years, before a settlement was reached in March. Halkbank was barred from entering transactions that benefit Iran and had to hire a compliance monitor to review its sanctions and anti-money-laundering programs.
The two NATO allies have also clashed in their differences of opinion related to Israel's operations in Gaza, Trump’s tariff policies, and Washington’s maintained block on F-35 fighter jet sales to Turkey while Ankara still holds Russian-made S-400 air defense systems.
Republican Sen. Rick Scott of Florida earlier this week said “Turkey is not our friend” as he showed support for the sanctions targeting firms in the country. “Bessent had to crack down on them for actively funding Iranian terrorists,” he claimed.
How corporations in other countries respond to the U.S. measures “is an important test” for the Trump Administration, Roush says, noting that despite Washington’s crackdown on international entities supporting the Iranian economy, some have shown they’re willing to continue doing business with Tehran.
"A lot of these smaller, more boutique firms… They're more informal. They tend to continue their trade ties or banking ties with Iran. The UAE has done, or well, they're trying to do a good job of severing these ties with Iran, but other states in the region, like Iraq and Azerbaijan and Turkey, are continuing to trade with Iran,” says Roush. “Iran is an important trading partner for them, and I think it's going to take a significant amount of diplomatic pressure to impose some kind of a full blockade of Iran.”
How Iran has responded to the aviation sanctions
Iran’s ambassador to the United Nations Gholamhossein Darzi on Wednesday argued that Washington’s sanctions amount to “economic terrorism” and “collective punishment,” according to Iran's Mehr news agency.
Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s Foreign Minister, dismissed the effectiveness of the “economic D-Day” campaign.
“After 47 years of sanctions, the U.S. went to war with Iran on behalf of Israel. The fallout has been disastrous for America, including its standing worldwide,” he said Tuesday. “After failing to achieve its aims through sanctions or war, Washington’s ‘novel’ solution is… more sanctions. Seriously?”
But experts say the ramped up economic pressure campaign will undoubtedly impact Iran in some way.
The aviation-related measures alone will “make it harder to transport materiel to keep Mahan Air going, and it'll contribute to regional isolation,” says Roush.
Furthermore, Iran is already feeling the economic impact of the conflict and the U.S. naval blockade on its ports in the Strait of Hormuz.
On Sep. 10, Iran’s Rial currency plummeted in value, hitting a record low open-market rate of 2.34 million rials to the dollar. Inflation has also climbed significantly, with reports indicating rural communities and low-income households are carrying the burden. The country lost around 630,000 manufacturing jobs in the first quarter of 2026, according to the Statistical Center of Iran.
“Ultimately, the Iranian people are likely to suffer, because the regime will continue its predatory practice of absorbing the economic resources of the country and channeling it toward its military efforts,” concludes Roush.

articles.title: US slaps new sanctions on networks 'aiding Iran's proxies'
articles.body:
