articles.title: Gateway or outpost? Inside Israel's growing footprint in Cyprus
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Gateway or outpost? Inside Israel's growing footprint in Cyprus
On the southern coast of Cyprus, the signs of a growing Israeli presence are becoming harder to miss.
There are new housing developments marketed to Israeli buyers, large parcels of land changing hands, political posters, and a network of schools, synagogues, kosher businesses, and other institutions serving a community that is no longer made up solely of tourists and second-home owners.
The result is an increasingly visible Israeli footprint on an island that has long relied on foreign capital to drive its property market.
Yet the scale and concentration of some projects have prompted a debate on the island: is this simply another wave of foreign investment, or is something more permanent taking shape?
A new wave of foreign investment
Cyprus’s economy has long depended on third-state investment, with successive schemes – including the controversial “golden passports” and golden visas – designed to attract capital, particularly into property.
Historically dominated by the United Kingdom and Russia, capital has more recently come from Lebanon, Ukraine, and Israel.
The golden visa scheme enables non-European Union (EU) nationals to obtain residency by investing €300,000 in property or a company, raising concerns over transparency and regulation.
Direct investment vis-à-vis Israel stood at around €3.5 billion in stock in 2025, with €308 million in transactions, according to preliminary data from the Central Bank of Cyprus.
Recent Israeli investments have involved large land purchases and projects combining housing developments with resorts and gated communities. In 2023, liberal Israeli newspaper Haaretz wondered whether Cyprus was becoming the “second Israel?”
Israel's growing exodus
The trend coincides with rising Israeli emigration. Since 2023, political tensions surrounding judicial reforms proposed by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition government, followed by the Gaza war, have fuelled mounting insecurity and pessimism about the country’s future.
“The justice reform from January 2023 was the first turning point. Many lost hope in the future of Israel. October 2023 confirmed this trend, and many decided to move,” Michael Harari, Israel’s former ambassador in Cyprus, told The New Arab.
Between 2023 and 2025, 270,000 citizens left Israel, a recent study based on data from the Israel Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS) found, highlighting particularly substantial emigration among highly educated and economically strong groups.
In Cyprus, this movement has translated into both relocation and investment – helping turn what was once largely a tourism and property relationship into a more visible presence.
Cyprus as a haven
In this troubled landscape, removed from regional convulsions, Cyprus has become “Israel’s favourite island escape” – less than an hour away by plane, relatively affordable and safe.
“Cyprus offers the closest escape,” Louisa Varaclas, director of the Israel Office within the Cyprus Tourism Ministry, told The New Arab.
Israel was Cyprus’s second-largest tourism market in 2025, accounting for 13% of all arrivals, or 600,000 visitors. The Israeli Embassy estimates that around 15,000 to 20,000 Israelis currently live in Cyprus, compared with 6,500 in 2018, although the exact number is difficult to determine because many hold European Union (EU) passports.
Geographical proximity, political ties, a favourable tax regime, business opportunities, and a sense of security have helped make the island attractive for residence and investment.
“Cyprus is a security partner,” Roee Kibrik, Director of Research from the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies (Mitvim), told The New Arab. For Israel’s strategic logic, he argues, the island can almost be understood as an extension of Israel’s security space - while the partnership also serves Cyprus’s security interests.
“Given that political and economic relations between Israel and Cyprus deepen, there will also be growing Israeli interest in tourism, residence, and investment in Cyprus,” Zenonas Tziarras, a lecturer in the Department of Turkish and Middle Eastern Studies from the University of Cyprus, told The New Arab.
Cyprus also offers a “gateway” to the European Union (EU), its market, its electricity and gas infrastructures and sea routes, but also its institutional structures and political channels, Kibrik argues.
From property to communities
The growing Israeli presence is particularly visible in coastal areas around Larnaca, Limassol, and Paphos, where Israelis have purchased property and marketed dedicated housing complexes. Jewish institutions, kosher businesses, and Hebrew-language services have expanded alongside them.
“Some definitely left Israel. Some others live in Cyprus while continuing to work in Israel, while others are moving part of their assets or establishing companies in Cyprus,” Kibrik says.
This trend has also fueled concerns over housing affordability. Property prices rose by 11.7% in Larnaca and 10.7% in Limassol between 2025 and 2026, with the Central Bank of Cyprus attributing part of the inflation to stronger demand from third-country investors, alongside construction and labour costs.
Harari admits there are tensions. “This migration is a natural process and contributes largely to the local economy. But of course, for a small place as Cyprus, these numbers are substantial, and you can also understand concerns from local populations because there is influence on property prices.”
The island’s role as a refuge during crises has further deepened these connections. In October 2023, 5,000 Israelis landed in Cyprus. During the Israel-Iran conflict in June 2025, 15,000 Israelis were stranded after airspace closure.
Chabad centres provided accommodation, food, and emergency assistance, illustrating how a network initially serving religious and tourist needs has also become part of the infrastructure supporting a growing Israeli community.
Chabad, a global Hasidic Jewish movement, operates around 4,000 centres in 100 countries. Publicly apolitical, recent investigations have documented support from parts of the movement for Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power), the far-right party led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
In Cyprus, Chabad operates six centres, alongside a synagogue, kindergarten, mikvah, kosher certification agency, a cemetery, and summer programmes. Its founder and Cyprus’s chief rabbi, Zeev Raskin, also promotes the development of resorts and tourist complexes designed to comply with Jewish law.
Gated communities and contested projects
Several projects have sparked controversy over planning and environmental regulation, the role of national and local authorities, and the longer-term character of this presence.
In Latchi, a large hotel complex completed the final stages of construction while licensing issues remained unresolved. In Polemidia, a €50 million Jewish school designed for up to 1,500 students has generated concerns over traffic and planning, while the municipality had not been involved in the process.
Its slated director, Rabbi Yehoshua Smukler, has described the project as the future “cornerstone” of Cyprus’s Jewish community.
In Trozena and Gerovasa, Hungarian-Israeli businessman Uriel Kertesz has proposed redeveloping abandoned villages into an “ecotourism” project combining homes, vineyards, a wellness centre and restored ruins. The project has faced environmental scrutiny, as the area falls within the Natura network of protected natural areas.
In Zygi, a 60,000-square-metre luxury development is marketed as a gated complex of residences serving the Jewish community. When announced in 2024 by property entrepreneur Daniel Morris Goldberg and Rabbi Ziv Raskin, the project was promoted as a “kosher slice” of Cyprus.
“Do we have closed communities, rather than absorbing individuals into the local culture?” Kibrik asks, pointing to an emerging debate over housing, culture, and the transformation of some areas.
The speed and concentration of Israeli investments distinguish them from the longer-established Russian presence, notes Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, Assistant Professor in Transitional Justice and Human Rights from the University of Central Lancashire - Cyprus.
“Russians have had a very long-standing presence on the island, which developed gradually, whereas Israelis have been much more sudden and economically aggressive, with entire areas being purchased. Russians are primarily based in Limassol and live within the city, whereas some Israelis have begun constructing gated communities, separating themselves within exclusive areas," Hadjigeorgiou tells The New Arab.
"There is also an oversensitivity here because of what is happening in Israel and Palestine and the history of Israelis settling on land, accompanied by violence and displacement, while the local history of occupation vis-à-vis Türkiye adds another layer.”
Theodosis Pipis, a doctoral candidate in History from the University of Leiden, puts the question more bluntly.
“Given these projects and the high concentration of land purchases happening swiftly in coastal and port cities, could Cyprus be falling under the auspices of some form of permanent or semi-permanent Israeli expansionism?”
Growing influence and public outrage
In July 2026, campaign posters for Gadi Eisenkot, former Israeli army chief-of-staff and candidate in Israel’s elections, popped up along highways around Larnaca airport, generating an unusual debate over Israel’s growing influence in Cyprus.
This event echoed wider concerns. “Israeli buyers are purchasing significant land parcels and strategic economic assets. This cannot but sound the alarm for us,” Stefanos Stefanou, a spokesperson for the Progressive Party of Working People (AKEL), warned in June 2025.
And this trend has become a significant issue across the political spectrum, from the election posters to the redevelopment of abandoned villages.
“It’s a topic most circles on the island discuss - no matter though you are from the left, the far-right, the centre, we can all see the growing Israeli presence on the island,” Pipis tells The New Arab.
Growing economic connections also involve powerful business interests. Cypriot-Israeli real estate businessman Yakir Gabay, whose fortune is estimated at around $4 billion, has become a prominent figure in Cyprus.
He is involved in an €856 million investment project around Limassol and recently purchased a 950,000-square-metre plot from the Bank of Cyprus for €28 million.
In February 2026, he also joined the executive committee of the 'Board of Peace'. He visits Israel frequently, operates behind the scenes, and has close personal and business ties to Jared Kushner and, as early as November 2023, reportedly submitted a reconstruction plan for Palestine.
Cyprus, alongside Greece, has recently become an essential part of Israel’s strategic environment. The relationship spans defence, military cooperation and energy, and has developed into a deeper strategic partnership.
Since June 2017, the Israeli military has regularly conducted exercises on the island, including air force, naval, and ground forces units, and intelligence and evacuation drills. The exercises have included simulations relevant to operations in southern Lebanon, making Cyprus a uniquely accessible training environment for Israel’s military.
“Of course, the deepening strategic relationship between both states has made Cyprus an attractive place to Israeli citizens, as a place to invest and live. Both come together,” Harari says.
Sylvain Henry is a writer based in Samos, Greece, and a master's graduate in sociology and political philosophy. He recently worked with the Cyprus Refugee Council
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: UK lawmakers urge Burnham to back ban on superintelligent AI after chilling warnings
articles.body:
More than 70 MPs and peers have urged Andy Burnham to back a ban on the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI) and lead an international movement to stop the technology after a week of warnings from experts of a 10% chance it could kill all humans.
Fifteen former government ministers, along with the former head of the civil service Robin Butler, senior Labour MPs including John McDonnell and leading Conservatives, Liberal Democrat and Scottish National party MPs have written to the prime minister. They urged him to throw the government’s weight behind a bill, tabled in the Commons on Tuesday, that would prohibit ASI – an as-yet-nonexistent AI that would outcompete human capabilities in most domains.
They have escalated their campaign to Downing Street after concerning statements from current and former AI insiders. Evan Hubinger, a senior employee at Anthropic, said he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity, and Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at Anthropic, who previously worked at OpenAI, quit on Tuesday with a warning that went viral, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”, they were “gambling with our lives” and were locked in a race for AI supremacy.
Alex Sobel, the Labour MP behind the bill, said he and other signatories – ranging from the children’s TV presenter Floella Benjamin to the former Conservative environment minister Zac Goldsmith and former Northern Ireland first minister Arlene Foster – want Burnham to foster “a clear framework where superintelligent AI cannot be created”. He added: “AI companies have made it clear that they will develop agents without constraint. They’re trying to develop superintelligence, while openly admitting there is a significant risk of human extinction.”
The bill mirrors legislation banning ASI promoted in Washington DC by Bernie Sanders, who this week said: “You’ve got to be a moron not to say slow it down.” It is backed by the Nobel prize-winning nuclear proliferation campaigner Beatrice Fihn and the leading Berkeley AI professor Stuart Russell, as well as Control AI, a transatlantic lobby group funded by the billionaire Skype co-founder and self-described “anti-extinctionist” Jaan Tallinn.
A ban on ASI in the UK, but not in the US or China where the frontier models are being created, risks having little impact. But the parliamentarians’ bill aims to pave the way to an international agreement. They call on Burnham to use next year’s UK presidency of the G20 to create “a coalition of the willing to tackle this national and international security threat”.
A government spokesperson said: “While we do not consider the measures proposed in the bill to be the right approach, we are exploring whether additional targeted interventions may be needed in future to address the most significant AI-related national security risks.”
Others have played down the risk, saying that ASI remains only theoretical and that guardrails could work to prevent the worst outcomes. Experts warn that these could include catastrophic cyber-attacks, novel biohazards and AIs in control of autonomous weaponry. This week’s wave of concern follows a spate of more minor but still worrying incidents involving unexpected misbehaviour by AI agents under training by OpenAI and Anthropic in which they broke out of training environments, secretly conspired and hacked into other systems.
Elon Musk, who runs xAI as part of his SpaceX empire, suggested without evidence that this week’s warnings of catastrophic risk were part of a “psyop” that “has been prepared for a long time”. The world’s richest man gave a different read on the state of AI, claiming: “AI+robots will more than double the global economy in less than 10 years.”
Anthropic revealed another incident of a rogue AI this week and said criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists had attempted to use its AI models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents. At its main rival, OpenAI, Paul Christiano, an AI adviser to the US government, joined the lab’s non-profit foundation and immediately warned the company was not on track to reduce the risk of “catastrophic” loss of control to an acceptable level.

articles.title: Canada sanctions eight Russians over deported Ukrainian children as only about 2,500 of more than 20,000 have come home
articles.body:
Canada has sanctioned eight people over Russia's deportation of Ukrainian children and their indoctrination and militarization, Ukrinform reported on 11 September. It is the second Canadian package this year built around the removal of children from occupied areas. The measure surfaced during Ukraine's presidential visit to Canada, at a moment when Kyiv's own register counts far more children taken than brought home.
Eight names, and what Ottawa says they did
Canada's foreign ministry says all eight took part, now or earlier, in unlawfully deporting and transferring Ukrainian children, and in subjecting them to indoctrination and militarization. The department published the eight names without setting out the posts they hold. Its own register dates the listing's entry into force to 4 September.
The listing is an administrative measure, not a criminal charge. In most cases, people in Canada and Canadians abroad may not deal in a listed person's property or provide them financial services. Breaking those rules is a criminal offense, investigated by the border agency and the federal police.
Canada pledges more than $1 billion for Ukraine’s critical air defense as Russia intensifies missile and drone attacks
Canada's Ukraine-related listings cover more than 3,500 individuals and entities across its Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and Moldova regulations. Its separate ship list reached 731 vessels in June, listed for shadow-fleet work moving sanctioned Russian oil, gas, and arms. The previous expansion, in August, hit a manufacturer of armored vehicles.
Thousands of children taken, about 2,000 home
Russia has deported or displaced 20,651 Ukrainian children since February 2022, and Ukraine has brought just over 2,000 of them home through the Bring Kids Back UA initiative. Officials believe the real figure is far higher.
Russian authorities have moved groups of Ukrainian teenagers through military-patriotic camps, occupation schools, and youth movements in occupied areas and inside Russia, and Ukraine has named the people running that work.

articles.title: BRICS: The gears of change keep grinding
articles.body:
BRICS: The gears of change keep grinding
BRICS leaders are meeting in New Delhi this weekend for the group’s 18th annual summit.
India took over the rotating chair of the group in January and has adopted a different tone. Rhetoric about de-dollarization and overhauling the current financial system has taken a back seat to more practical considerations of economic connectivity.
The summit comes against a mixed backdrop. On the one hand, Chinese President Xi Jinping will be in attendance in what will be his first visit to India in seven years. This underscores the importance Beijing attaches to BRICS. Also traveling to Delhi is Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On the other hand, recently joined BRICS members UAE and Iran have found themselves on opposite sides of the hostilities in the Middle East. A two-day meeting of BRICS foreign ministers in New Delhi in May concluded without a joint statement due to divergent views on the Middle East, and this weekend’s summit will be taking place in the shadow of this tension.
Nevertheless, as trade ties among key BRICS countries keep growing, the methodical work of creating new financial channels and architecture continues apace. BRICS is slowly but surely building an entire institutional ecosystem for trade, investment, and settlement. It is a process often unfolding without loud pronouncements and far from news cycles.
RT takes a look at what’s going on in BRICS these days.
Progress on payments
Perhaps the most important tangible proposals on the agenda for this year’s summit are ones to link the payment systems of BRICS countries.
There are two tracks for this.
The first is the BRICS Pay project. This is an effort to create an interoperable payment system across BRICS countries that would connect national and commercial payment systems with the aim of supporting settlements in national currencies. BRICS Pay exists at the pilot level but has not yet been rolled out commercially across the bloc.
When implemented, it will make sending money between BRICS countries more like making a domestic electronic payment rather than sending money through a chain of banks and currencies. Currently, for example, if an Indian company buys something from a Brazilian company, the cross-border payment can involve such hassles as correspondent banks and currency conversions – not to mention additional costs.
According to Kremlin aide Kirill Dmitriev, an agreement on BRICS Pay is forthcoming at the summit, where a specific emphasis will be placed on financial questions.
“We are focusing specifically on the financial track. We lead the group responsible for cooperation on financial issues, and payments are a very important part of this,” he said.
This does not necessarily mean, however, that the entire BRICS Pay architecture is about to become operational, but it does mean that the project might receive a large push.
The second track is the proposed linking of members’ central-bank digital currencies (CBDC) for cross-border payments, which India has reportedly included on the agenda of the event.
Linking up the CBDCs of BRICS countries would make the central-bank-issued digital money interoperable across countries. This initiative represents a deeper level in the financial plumbing than BRICS Pay. It would allow cross-border transactions to be settled more directly and with fewer intermediaries and steps. It would also represent an additional settlement route outside the Western-centered architecture.
Importantly, however, this is explicitly not being framed as the creation of a BRICS currency, an initiative that has at times been the subject of speculation.
The CBDC link-up project remains at the discussion stage.
BRICS trade
Trade within the group continues to grow. Intra-BRICS exports totaled about $1.2 trillion in 2025. India’s trade with the other BRICS members, for example, reached around $416 billion in 2025, growing at nearly 10% annually from 2021–25.
Up for endorsement by leaders at the summit is the BRICS Economic Partnership Strategy 2030, which is an extension of an existing BRICS economic strategy document that, among other things, focuses on trade and investment, the digital economy, and financial cooperation.
A major aim of the initiative is to facilitate a broad reduction in institutional friction for economic activity within the group. It also emphasizes supply-chain resilience and support for small and medium-sized businesses, among other areas.
It is this type of unglamorous nitty-gritty work that can provide the foundation for BRICS economic infrastructure to eventually match the size and scale of the group’s economies.
Meanwhile, the New Development Bank, established by BRICS in 2015, has now approved roughly $43 billion in lending. While still relatively small in scale, the bank is an example of a BRICS institution that is now up and running.
Energy ties
The crucial energy trade continues to expand as well, notwithstanding Western attempts to suppress Russian exports of oil and gas.
India’s imports of Russian crude reached 2.47 million barrels per day in July 2026, a record 50.8% of India’s total crude imports and 62.4% above the figure from the year prior. For April–July 2026, Russia supplied 43.25% of India’s crude imports, up from 37% a year earlier. Russia remains China’s largest crude oil supplier and the two countries continue to develop energy ties.
Meanwhile, Russia’s recently launched greenfield Vostok Oil, a massive cluster of fields deep in the Arctic, is expected to greatly expand Russia’s energy trade with Asia via the Northern Sea Route, although it will be years before volumes are expected to reach capacity. Nevertheless, this represents a strategically important route that bypasses the fraught Middle East.
Nuclear cooperation has also been a prominent part of the broader BRICS energy and technology agenda. China, India, and Russia are all major powers in civilian nuclear energy and have sought to boost cooperation in recent years.
The bigger context
BRICS has sometimes moved more slowly than proponents would like and has at times been derided, especially in Western policy circles, for a perceived lack of concrete action.
Some expectations placed on the group may have been unrealistic. Financial architecture certainly has enormous inertia, and incumbent systems with decades of accumulated infrastructure and well-established channels are not displaced quickly, even when the need for alternative mechanisms becomes apparent.
Meanwhile, the crisis in the Middle East, in which BRICS members Iran and the UAE are at odds, is being portrayed as a challenge for unified action.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov acknowledged that the differences between Iran and the UAE had a “negative impact” on efforts to prepare a joint declaration, although he expressed optimism that diplomatic efforts could bridge the gap.
However, behind the scenes and at a remove from the vicissitudes of politics, work continues to create the infrastructure that will provide nations representing half of the world’s population and 40% of GDP greater economic autonomy. Developing this infrastructure is also at the heart of efforts to create alternatives to Western-dominated systems.
The on-ramp may be long, but once this infrastructure is in place at scale, global financial channels could start looking very different.
This weekend's summit is another step in this direction.

articles.title: Sweden’s NATO missions are at risk if the left wins election, warns PM Kristersson
articles.body:
STOCKHOLM — With two days to go before Sweden’s knife-edge general election, Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has a warning for Europe: Don’t trust the left on defense.
His country has been almost totally united in its support for Ukraine and in backing the decision — after decades of neutrality — to join NATO two years ago. But speaking to POLITICO in the capital Stockholm, the center-right Moderate party leader argued that Europe should wake up to the security risks of the rival left-wing bloc taking power — which polls suggest may happen.
Asked what's at stake for Europe in Sunday’s vote, Kristersson said: “I would say security policy. If the left side would win, two out of three, or two out of four parties voted against the Swedish NATO membership. I mean, that is a real, real thing.”
Advertisement
He continued: “That means a government that will not be able to make the domestic decisions needed to fulfill our NATO obligations, for example — like spending, like all the missions.”
Sweden became NATO’s newest member in 2024, the national mood having shifted in favor of taking sides in the face of Vladimir Putin’s territorial aggression in Europe. That decision was “a big thing” for the country of 10.6 million people, which was neutral during both world wars and throughout the Cold War, Kristersson said.
“But after becoming a member, we have made a NATO-related decision every month in government,” the prime minister added. “And if government is not united, they simply cannot make the decisions.”
Kristersson speaks to reporters on Sept. 11, 2026 in Stockholm. | Tim Ross/POLITICO
Since becoming a member of the alliance, Sweden has sent hundreds of troops to join a NATO force in Latvia, pledged warships for patrolling the Baltic Sea and deployed Gripen fighter jets to police the skies in the region.
Asked if he believed support for Ukraine would be in doubt too, Kristersson said: “I hope, really not, because we have been united on Ukraine — with one single exception. The Left Party voted against the very first support package to Ukraine. From that [point] on, eight parties out of eight have been united.”
Kristersson’s comments follow a pointed intervention from Social Democrat opposition leader Magdalena Andersson, who demanded the PM come clean about his allies’ links to Russia in a POLITICO interview published this week.
Advertisement
Until recently, Sunday’s upcoming vote seemed like it would be a comfortable victory for Andersson’s Social Democrats and their political allies in smaller parties on the left. But their poll lead shrank dramatically in the past two weeks to as low as 2.6%, within the statistical margin of error.
Far-right friends
Kristersson’s center-right coalition has been governing for the past four years with the support of the far-right Sweden Democrats. He defended his decision to cooperate with a party opponents claim is too extreme despite its internal efforts to clean up its past neo-Nazi links.
“I have full respect for the fact that there are eight parties in the Swedish parliament,” said Kristersson. “None of these parties are even close to a majority of their own. If you cannot unite parties on specific topics and ambitions, then you will simply not get anything done at all.”
Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson, the first woman to serve as Swedish PM, leads the polls. | Tim Ross/POLITICO
Under leader Jimmie Åkesson, the Sweden Democrats are in second place behind Andersson’s Social Democrats in the polls. Åkesson has said he’s eyeing up the chance of becoming prime minister at the next vote, due in 2030.
If Kristersson returns as prime minister after Sunday’s election, he has said he’s ready to give Sweden Democrat politicians roles as ministers in his government for the first time. It would be a major change for Sweden — and the left-wing bloc has campaigned against it.
Kristersson suggested that being part of a team would limit the opportunities for any individual ministers to go rogue with extremist policies.
“In Sweden, we have a collective decision-making process in government,” he said. “I would never say that one minister is not important, but every minister is part of a team that jointly makes all the decisions — so there is very little room for people to play in a role of their own.
“And since I will be the person that is forming that government, and the person that will appoint every one of them, I can guarantee you that it will only be very skilled and experienced and people with good judgment that would be part of my government.”

articles.title: Why a Divided BRICS Poses No Challenge to America
articles.body:
When the leaders of BRICS, the bloc of emerging economies, gather in New Delhi on Saturday for their 18th summit, they will have plenty to talk about. The group began with Brazil, Russia, India and China, then added South Africa in 2010. It has since expanded to include 11 countries.
The leaders and diplomats of BRICS member states are meeting in New Delhi to consider how their combined political and economic muscle might be used to build an alternative to the American-led global order. In some ways, President Donald Trump’s refusal to allow America play its traditional postwar leadership role has created new opportunities for the bloc. Yet its ambitions remain constrained by an inconvenient fact: India, China, Russia and Brazil do not align particularly well.
Here are the dynamics to watch this weekend. India, the host, wants the summit to accomplish as much as possible without antagonizing the United States. India continues to value the stability of its relationship with Washington, particularly as a counterbalance to China’s expanding influence in Asia and beyond. India, along with Brazil, has also resisted Russian and Chinese calls for a common BRICS currency and new lending to sanctions-hit Russia.
For its part, China is seeking to extend its global influence. For President Xi Jinping, this summit is another stage in an international roadshow that has included a leading role at this year’s Shanghai Cooperation Organization gathering in Kyrgyzstan, a visit to Egypt to help mediate the ongoing war in the Middle East and, later this month, a state visit to the White House.
In Delhi, Xi hopes to present China as a stable, predictable alternative to American influence. He will also seek to erode the dollar’s continuing dominance as the world’s principal reserve currency by promoting more channels for nondollar lending, the wider use of the renminbi to settle trade, and progress toward linking digital payment systems, an effort India has long resisted.
Given the sometimes violent border clashes between China and India in recent years, observers will also be watching Xi’s and Modi’s body language closely. Despite their differences on key agenda items, they are likely to be all smiles. Neither has an interest in airing grievances. India, as host, wants a smooth show. China, which will host next year’s summit, also wants a positive atmosphere. And Xi’s overriding goal is to present his country as a mature and constructive global leader.
Russia, of course, wants whatever diplomatic, political, and economic support it can get for its stalemated war with Ukraine. Brazil, meanwhile, hopes to forge new economic linkages and reaffirm its commitment to being a full BRICS partner, even as some fear that a Flavio Bolsonaro victory in next month’s presidential election could undermine the country’s commitment to the bloc.
The founders will not be the only delegations in attendance. Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, all new members, will be there, introducing fresh tensions into the agenda and some awkward photo calls. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the UAE’s leader Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, however, are expected to dispatch lesser officials in their place.
The central question is how the summit’s final communiqué will address the war. The recent Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit produced a final document that included implicit criticism of the United States and Israel. We will see whether the UAE delegation allows for similar language from Delhi.
Whatever emerges from the gathering, BRICS is unlikely to become an anti-American or anti-Western power bloc anytime soon. Its clout is already limited by the rivalry between China and India. The four founding members also have divergent interests whenever a conflict carries major consequences for energy markets: Russia and Brazil are major exporters who want higher energy prices while China and India, as major importers, prefer lower ones.
Equally important, the bloc now includes American treaty allies or longstanding partners, among them the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia. Their presence will impose another check on BRICS’s ambitions. All of them want to hedge against dependence on an increasingly unpredictable America. Most of them also want to preserve a stable relationship with the global superpower.

Zelensky: Canada’s anti-ballistic sanctions could take effect in October

“I thank Canada for imposing sanctions on all those individuals and all those enterprises that Russia uses to prevent the return of our Ukrainian children, stolen from our land, from our occupied cities and villages,” he said.

articles.title: Why tens of thousands of Hasidic Jews are flocking to Ukraine – and why they are dancing
articles.body:
Why tens of thousands of Hasidic Jews are flocking to Ukraine – and why they are dancing
Tens of thousands of Hasidic Jews are flocking to central Ukraine, praying, singing, and dancing as they prepare to mark the Jewish New Year.
The annual pilgrimage draws thousands of visitors from around the world.
But who are they, why do they travel to a relatively small Ukrainian city every year, and are they still coming despite the conflict?
Who are the Hasidic Jews?
Hasidism is a movement within Orthodox Judaism that emerged in Eastern Europe in the 18th century. Over time, it developed into a number of groups with their own traditions and religious leaders.
Most of those making the annual journey to Uman are followers of the Breslov branch. Their connection to the city goes back to the man who founded the movement more than 200 years ago – Rabbi Nachman.
Who was Rabbi Nachman?
Nachman was born in 1772 in what is now Ukraine and was a great-grandson of Israel Baal Shem Tov, who is regarded as the founder of the Hasidic movement.
He founded the Breslov branch and emphasized prayer, simplicity, and joy. He also placed particular importance on his followers gathering with him for Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year.
Large groups of Hasidim are crossing into Ukraine and heading to Uman for Rosh Hashanah. Several thousand are already there. By September 11, when the Jewish New Year begins, organizers expect up to 40,000 pilgrims from Israel, the US and around the world. War, missile risk,… pic.twitter.com/eklA9ZzENB
— Iuliia Mendel (@IuliiaMendel) September 8, 2026
Nachman died in Uman in 1810 and was buried there. His followers continued gathering in the city after his death, beginning a tradition that eventually developed into today’s mass annual pilgrimage.
How did Uman become a pilgrimage center?
Uman is a relatively small city in central Ukraine’s Cherkasy Region, around 200km south of Kiev. Its population stood at just over 80,000 before the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, while the annual pilgrimage brings tens of thousands of additional visitors.
Nachman moved to Uman only months before his death. Historical accounts say he chose the city because thousands of Jews had been killed there during a massacre in 1768 and wanted to be buried near the victims.
Uman later became home to a large Jewish community. Jews accounted for 59% of its population by 1897. The community was devastated during World War II, when around 17,000 Jews were killed after Nazi forces occupied the city.
Visits to Nachman’s grave continued on a much smaller scale during the Soviet period before growing substantially after the collapse of the USSR.
What is Rosh Hashanah?
This year, Rosh Hashanah begins at sunset on September 11 and ends after nightfall on September 13. Unlike the secular New Year, it is primarily a religious holiday centered on prayer and reflection.
The holiday has particular importance for Breslov followers because Nachman considered their annual Rosh Hashanah gathering especially important. After his death, his followers continued meeting in Uman during the holiday, explaining why the city sees its largest influx of pilgrims at this time of year.
Why all the dancing?
The singing and dancing seen on Uman’s streets are not required Rosh Hashanah rituals.
Music and dancing are common at Hasidic gatherings, while Rabbi Nachman placed particular emphasis on joy. His followers therefore often combine prayer with communal singing and dancing during their time in Uman.
Do pilgrims still come despite the conflict?
Yes. Tens of thousands have continued making the journey despite the hostilities and official travel warnings.
Around 35,000 pilgrims visited Uman in both 2023 and 2024, while more than 35,000 traveled there in 2025, according to Ukrainian officials and media reports. Ukrainian authorities expect as many as 40,000 this year.
Ukraine travel warning
Last week, the US Embassy in Kiev issued a security alert recommending that Americans not travel to Uman, citing the risk of airstrikes, martial law, and movement restrictions. The embassy also warned US-Ukrainian male dual nationals that they may be unable to leave the country and could be subject to conscription. Ukraine has ended an exemption that previously allowed certain Ukrainian men living abroad to leave the country.
Security has been stepped up for this year’s gathering. Israeli police officers have arrived in Uman to work alongside Ukrainian law enforcement in areas where pilgrims are staying and gathering, according to police in Ukraine’s Cherkasy Region.
The pilgrimage has persisted through earlier disruptions as well. In 2020, pilgrims attempted to reach Uman despite Covid-19 border and travel restrictions.

articles.title: BRICS 2026: India charts its own course between Russia and the West
articles.body:
BRICS 2026: India charts its own course between Russia and the West
The 18th BRICS Summit, opening in New Delhi on Friday, will test not only the geopolitical resilience of the largest grouping in the non-Western world, but also the maturity of Indian diplomacy.
India has set itself an extraordinarily difficult task of trying to pour the oil of reconciliation onto the increasingly stormy waters of world politics.
The theme of its 2026 BRICS presidency, “Building for Sustainability, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainable Development,” might sound hopelessly optimistic as the Ukraine conflict and sanctions against Russia continue, the US and Iran remain locked in confrontation, Western pressure on China is growing, Africa and Latin America face what BRICS countries regard as neo-colonial practices, and while trade and technology wars are multiplying.
Against such a background, talk of innovation and sustainable development can seem detached from reality, yet this is precisely where India sees a role for itself; as divisions between rival centers of power deepen, New Delhi is attempting the diplomatic equivalent of walking a tightrope. It believes its longstanding principle of “strategic autonomy” will allow it not merely to keep its balance, but to make a wider contribution to international stability.
That approach is central to understanding India’s BRICS presidency, given that among the BRICS states, India occupies a unique position. It maintains strategic partnerships with the United States and Western European countries whose policies increasingly seek to contain Russia and China, while, at the same time, New Delhi has refused Western demands to distance itself from Moscow.
India consequently doesn’t regard BRICS as an anti-Western alliance. For sure it sees the grouping as non-Western, but not inherently antagonistic towards the West, and this leaves New Delhi caught between two fires.
Some within BRICS may accuse India of being insufficiently willing to confront the West, while Western governments repeatedly criticize India for maintaining close relations with Russia, often invoking its status as the world’s largest democracy.
Shortly before the summit, Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar offered a characteristically pointed defense of this strategic autonomy at an international forum in Finland.
Asked by a British moderator whether cooperation with Russia was immoral, Jaishankar replied that no European country had ever been attacked with Indian weapons, while European weapons had been used against India.
The exchange neatly captured New Delhi’s position as India has no intention of allowing either side to dictate its foreign policy.
Being caught between two fires is rarely comfortable, but India’s strategy isn’t simply to avoid getting burnt; instead, it intends to draw warmth from both while retaining the freedom to choose its own course.
That is both the risk and the ambition behind India’s BRICS presidency.
This article was first published by Kommersant, and was translated and edited by the RT team.

articles.title: Egypt to protect Suez Canal from Houthi Bab al-Mandeb takeover
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Egypt activates plans to protect Suez Canal from Houthi Bab al-Mandeb takeover
Egypt has formed a crisis team to monitor developments around the Bab al-Mandab Strait after Houthi forces reached the strategically located Yemeni island of Mayyun, an informed Egyptian source has told The New Arab.
Mayyun, also known as Perim, lies at the southern entrance to Bab al-Mandab, one of the world's most important shipping chokepoints, connecting the Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea and, further north, the Suez Canal.
The Egyptian source said Cairo was concerned about the potential impact of the latest military developments on shipping in the Red Sea and traffic through the Suez Canal, a major source of revenue for Egypt.
The crisis team was established urgently after Egyptian authorities received reports of developments around the strait and was continuing to assess the situation, the source said.
Egypt believes the latest development represents a different type of threat from previous Houthi attacks on shipping, which have largely involved missiles and drones.
The source said the movement of fighting to territory immediately surrounding Bab al-Mandab had changed the nature of the risk.
Cairo had activated existing channels of communication with the Houthis to establish what was happening on the ground, clarify the objectives behind their movements and determine whether they were linked to the wider regional escalation, the source added.
Egypt was also in contact with the United States, Saudi Arabia and Iran in an attempt to contain the situation and prevent developments in Yemen from becoming a sustained threat to Red Sea shipping.
The source said Cairo had warned against further escalation because of the strategic importance of Bab al-Mandab.
Egypt viewed security in the strait as directly connected to its own national security and to the operation of the Suez Canal, rather than simply as a Yemeni or regional issue, the source said.
“The central message” in Cairo's diplomatic contacts was the need to prevent escalation and preserve the security of navigation, according to the source.
The source warned that turning Bab al-Mandab into a direct arena of confrontation between regional and international powers would have repercussions far beyond Yemen, potentially affecting the Red Sea, the Suez Canal and the global economy.
Former Egyptian Assistant Foreign Minister Mohamed Hegazy told The New Arab that the Houthi advance towards Bab al-Mandab, including their arrival in Dhubab and Mayyun, represented a significant change in the Red Sea security environment.
He said the significance of the development went beyond the capture of territory inside Yemen because of Bab al-Mandab's role in international shipping.
The narrow strait forms a key part of the sea route linking the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean with the Red Sea and Suez Canal.
Hegazy said the Houthi presence in such strategically sensitive areas increased the risks for commercial shipping and could give the group greater leverage over maritime traffic without requiring it to formally close the strait.
An increase in the perceived security risk alone could affect decisions by shipping companies and insurers and prompt changes to international trade routes, he said.
Hegazy warned that continued fighting close to Bab al-Mandab risked accelerating the militarisation of important maritime routes and further destabilising regional trade and energy flows.
The warning comes as several strategically important waterways in the region are already facing heightened tensions.
Egypt has particular concerns because disruption at Bab al-Mandab can directly affect traffic heading north through the Red Sea towards the Suez Canal.
Sustained disruption could therefore have consequences both for global trade and Egypt's economy, Hegazy said.
He argued that protecting the Red Sea required greater co-ordination among countries bordering it, as well as efforts to strengthen the stability of states along the maritime route.
Strategic locations in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden should not be turned into instruments of regional rivalry, he added.
Hegazy said any response should not rely solely on military measures, but should also involve diplomatic and political efforts to prevent the war in Yemen from expanding.
The priority, he said, should be to maintain freedom of navigation and prevent Bab al-Mandab from becoming an open arena of conflict threatening both regional security and the global economy.

articles.title: F-35 jets: fixed-price scandal will have no immediate consequences
articles.body:
F-35 jets: fixed-price scandal will have no immediate consequences
A Swiss parliamentary report on the absence of a fixed-price agreement for the procurement of new F-35 fighter jets from the US has sparked controversy. For now, however, no changes are expected, while former Defence Minister Viola Amherd has yet to comment.
Centre-right parties, which hold a majority in parliament, have made clear that they are not keen on a parliamentary committee of inquiry (CPI) into the procurement issue, while the Greens are pushing for this solution.
According to the House of Representative’s Committee on the Examination of Public Accounts (GPK-N), no flat-rate fixed price has been agreed with the US, as stated in a report published on Tuesday. The Swiss defence ministry has repeatedly assured the public that 36 American-made F-35A fighter jets would be delivered at a fixed price of CHF6 billion ($7.5 billion).
The new parliamentary report has sparked concerns in all parties in Switzerland. “The impact on Switzerland’s image is catastrophic,” Green lawmaker Clarence Chollet told the Keystone-ATS news agency.
Swiss People’s Party leader Thomas Aeschi declared: “We need to ask and clarify some fundamental questions. Who was in charge of the dossier? Was the law firm supervised, or did it act independently?”
For its part, the centre-right Radical-Liberal Party is calling for the restoration of trust between the government and parliament. Lawmakers must have access to clear information when the process is of such importance, it says.
More
Swiss government criticised for F-35 price failings
No legal consequences
As for any legal consequences, Andreas Stöckli, professor of constitutional and administrative law at the University of Fribourg says “it is difficult to assess whether federal administration staff face any risk”.
“The requirements for financial liability on the part of Swiss administration staff are stringent,” he says.
It would be necessary, for example, to prove that there was unlawful conduct, and that the act was committed intentionally or through gross negligence, Stöckli told Keystone-ATS. In such a case, separate legal proceedings would have to be initiated. For the same reasons, the law firms involved in the F-35 procurement process should not be subject to legal proceedings either.
More
Renewed controversy in Switzerland over US fighter jets – explained
Amherd remains silent
When contacted by Keystone-ATS, Viola Amherd said she had already commented on the matter and would not be making any further statements regarding the allegations raised in the report.
The former defence minister from canton Valais, who is a member of the Centre Party, is unlikely to be held responsible, even though the negotiations relating to the purchase contract fell within her remit. According to the Greens, “such a fiasco cannot be attributed to the responsibility of a single person”.
Vincent Martenet, a lecturer in constitutional law at the University of Lausanne, noted that “members of the Federal Council enjoy absolute immunity for statements made before parliament”. In short, there remains only one option: a political one, via the creation of an parliamentary committee of inquiry (CPI) into the affair.
More
Pentagon ‘blocked’ critical F-35 fighter jet report
A CPI? Unlikely
The Greens are exploring this possibility and could put forward a motion during the autumn session of parliament in Bern.
However, the chances of persuading parties on the right to establish a CPI are slim. According to Pierre-Alain Fridez, a former Socialist lawmaker, “most parliamentarians will feel that the contracts have been misinterpreted. I fear they will stop there,” he said told the 24 heures newspaper.
The Social Democrats, for their part, expect the Federal Council to investigate whether any false statements liable to criminal prosecution were made in what it calls a colossal fiasco. The left is therefore likely to refuse to consider the request for an additional credit of almost CHF400 million for the 30 F-35s that are planned.
According to parliamentarian Benoît Gaillard, more time is needed “to shed light on the matter”.
“In our democratic state, it is a disgrace that a procurement worth over CHF6 billion, grudgingly accepted by the public, has been so badly managed,” said Clarence Chollet.

articles.title: Iranian, South Korean FMs hold phone call as protesters in Seoul oppose Hormuz deployment
articles.body:
Iranian, South Korean FMs hold phone call as protesters in Seoul oppose Hormuz deployment
TEHRAN — Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his South Korean counterpart, Cho Hyeon, spoke by phone on Friday. The two top diplomats discussed bilateral relations, the broader conflict in West Asia, and the situation around the Strait of Hormuz amid US military adventurism in the region.
The high-level diplomatic outreach highlights the significance of direct communication between Tehran and Seoul, coming on the heels of reports that South Korea is assessing whether to send troops to the Strait of Hormuz.
South Korean defense authorities disclosed that they had dispatched a specialized fact-finding mission to assess the situation on the ground in Hormuz. While official spokespersons in Seoul were quick to stress that no final decision had been made regarding any deployment, South Korea had previously acknowledged that it was actively considering “contributions” to US security efforts along the vital maritime corridor, provided that its own military readiness was not compromised.
Under South Korean constitutional law, should Seoul decide to deploy armed forces to the strait, the executive branch cannot act unilaterally; it would require formal parliamentary approval by a majority vote in the National Assembly—a hurdle that grows increasingly steep as public opposition intensifies.
Public outrage and street protests in Seoul
Dozens of South Korean anti-war activists, civil society leaders, and ordinary citizens gathered across from the massive United States embassy compound in Seoul on Wednesday to demand that their government unequivocally reject Washington’s pressure to deploy troops to the strategic Strait of Hormuz, fiercely slamming the ongoing campaign as an “illegal war”. The protesters unfurled banners and waved signs bearing powerful messages such as “Do not join a war of aggression”. They voiced their collective indignation as South Korean political and military leaders continue to weigh a potential “contribution” to the waterway’s security at the behest of the White House.
With passions running high against foreign military entanglements, the crowd echoed a resounding plea directly toward the presidential office: “We cannot send our young people into a sea of death!” Speaking outside the embassy, Jung Kyung-jik of People’s Solidarity for Participatory Democracy affirmed that Iranian concerns are grounded in legal reality: “As Iran has said, the deployment of our troops to the region would amount to direct participation in an illegal war”.
Choi Young-ok from Korean Peace Solidarity for Sovereignty and Reunification added, “Sending our troops to an illegal war waged by the United States is unacceptable... There is no reason for us to send troops when no other country has done so or said it would.”
The prospect of South Korea's potential military involvement in the Persian Gulf has drawn strong warnings from authorities in Iran, who have made it clear that any foreign intervention alongside hostile American forces will not go unanswered. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei has emphasized that such involvement would amount to “direct” support for the United States and would inevitably lead to serious consequences.

articles.title: Tusk warns of future attacks after ‘direct threat’ averted at Poland-Ukraine border
articles.body:
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk attends a press conference after a meeting of the Visegrád Group leaders in Bratislava, on Sept. 10, 2026. | Tomas Benedikovic/AFP via Getty Images
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a ‘direct threat’ was averted at a border crossing with Ukraine on Wednesday night and warned of further incidents linked to Russia in the near future.
His comments came just one day after a Russian drone hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, killing two people and wounding several others.
“Last night, thanks to cooperation between our services and their Ukrainian counterparts, a direct threat to a border crossing was averted,” Tusk said in a press conference after a meeting of the Visegrád Group leaders in Bratislava Thursday.
Advertisement
Tusk did not provide any further details about the nature of the threat or which of the 18 border crossings between Poland and Ukraine was affected.
The prime minister added that the incident was just a taste of what is to come and noted he had received a “fairly precise report” from the CIA regarding possible events in the coming months.
“We must anticipate various scenarios; both Poland and all of Europe need to be prepared for different possibilities concerning the situation not only on the Russian-Ukrainian front but also along the EU’s eastern flank.”
The incident at the border crossing between Moldova and Ukraine’s Odesa region left two people dead, causing President Maia Sandu to call for further European air defense support for Ukraine.
Russia also struck a Moldova-Ukraine border crossing in August.
“As you know, Russia has already resorted to provocative attacks on border crossings—for instance, in Moldova. We expect similar actions targeting border crossings with Ukraine in other countries, including Poland,” said Tusk.
Advertisement
In August, after a briefing with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, he warned that “escalation from Russia’s side is progressing,” and called for more air support for Ukraine as it is “crucial for our security.”
He said the next six months would be decisive and made it clear that provocations against NATO members should not be ruled out.
The CIA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Myanmar Rebels Strike Russian-Made Yak-130 With FPV Drone
articles.body:
Myanmar’s People’s Defence Forces struck a Russian-made Yak-130 trainer and light attack aircraft with an FPV drone at Tada-U airfield, south of Mandalay.
The footage was shared on X by journalist Thomas van Linge.
The drone struck the aircraft’s nose, which houses part of its onboard electronics and flight control systems.
The Yak-130 is a two-seat jet trainer and light attack aircraft developed by the Russian Yakovlev Design Bureau. It is designed to train combat aircraft pilots and can also be used as a light attack aircraft for engaging ground targets.
Myanmar 🇲🇲: PDF resistance sources published footage which showed FPV drones damage four junta jets at the Tada-U airbase, south of Mandalay.
Resistance forces just took their drone warfare to the next level. pic.twitter.com/8FAgZygKIo
— Thomas van Linge (@ThomasVLinge) September 10, 2026
Myanmar received a total of 20 Yak-130 aircraft from Russia, delivered in batches between 2017 and 2021. The country has already lost one or two aircraft of this type.
Following the 2021 military coup, the junta began using these aircraft extensively as light attack platforms, carrying out airstrikes with unguided missiles and bombs against rebel forces and civilian targets.
The People’s Defence Force is the armed wing of Myanmar’s National Unity Government, formed to fight against the ruling military junta.
